These are things that silently fail. They lived in chronological place in this

which cost real time during the 2026-07-28 crash recovery. They live here now.

**ADMISSION + EVICTION RULE FOR THIS BLOCK (read before adding to it).**
A trap ENTERS when it has cost us at least once. A trap LEAVES when the hazard is
**structurally eliminated** — tooling fixed, command wrapped, check automated —
not merely when it is well known. An entry that can only be honoured by
remembering to be careful is a **standing bug, not a standing note**, and should
carry a ticket. Rationale: an append-only chronology fails by being unread (this
file hit 0.6% effective readership); a head edited in place fails by ACCRETING
until it is skimmed, which rebuilds the same failure one level up, inside the fix
for it. The only pressure that keeps it short is that the way to evict an entry
is to FIX THE THING. **Review this block whenever it passes ~40 lines.**

**PROVENANCE RULE FOR EVERY CLAIM IN THIS FILE.**
Record how a claim was obtained, not just the claim: did the writer OBSERVE it
(ran a command) or was the writer TOLD it (relayed by an agent)? Mark the second
kind explicitly — "reported by EM at 11:29, not independently checked." Trigger on
SOURCE, not on confidence: "did I run something?" is mechanical and always
answerable, while "am I sure?" fails exactly when the source is credible, which is
the class that actually bites. Provenance's job is to PRICE a re-audit — a bare
claim gives a hurried reader no signal that re-derivation is even needed.
**Corollary — name IMMUTABLE referents.** SHA not branch; exact path not "the
tree"; counts accompanied by the names that produced them. A mutable referent
("HEAD", "current main", "the worktree") makes a later re-derivation return a
different TRUE answer, with no way to tell whether the record was wrong or the
world moved.

1. **`scion message` recipient needs the `user:` prefix.** `scion message
   --non-interactive ptone "..."` and `...ptone@google.com "..."` BOTH fail
   silently — they print generic flag help, no error, no send confirmation.
   Correct form: `user:ptone`. (First hit 03:1x 2026-07-28, hit AGAIN at 22:4x
   by the post-crash session that had read only the tail of this file.)

2. **`scion message` to a `user:` recipient silently fails above 2048 bytes.**
   Same symptom as #1 — prints flag help, does not send, exit status looks fine.
   Measured boundary is CONTENT-DEPENDENT, not a clean 2048: 1974 bytes sent,
   2011 bytes FAILED, on different text. Do not tune to the edge — **keep
   user-facing messages under ~1800 bytes and always check the output.**
   (I burned three send attempts re-trimming 2456 -> 2161 -> 2011 -> 1723
   because I'd recorded a single-probe boundary as if it were a constant. A
   limit measured on one input is not a constant; that is form (6) again.)
   Earlier single-probe reading, kept for provenance: 2000 sent, 2050 did not.
   **This limit is specific
   to `user:` recipients — a 2950-byte message to an AGENT delivered fine.** So
   briefs/rulings to agents are unconstrained; only user-facing updates need
   splitting into <2000-byte parts. **ALWAYS check the output for "Message sent
   ... via Hub" rather than assuming the send worked** — I sent a 2115-byte
   update believing it went out, ten minutes after discovering the limit.
   Do NOT bisect message limits against a live user inbox (ptone got five
   truncated fragments this way) — probe against a scratch agent instead.

2b. **ptone's standing comms preference: Discord, with EXPLICIT flags.**
   `scion message --non-interactive --channel discord --thread-id
   1528900732965748836 user:ptone "..."` — do not rely on default routing.

3. **A state file's last-write time is a LOWER BOUND on a crash, never the
   crash time.** Control-plane death is not container stop. In the 07-28 crash
   the control plane died ~13:13 and agent containers kept committing work
   until ~14:49 — 96 minutes later. Reasoning from the log's last write biases
   every recovery conclusion toward pessimism.

4. **In a recovery, the log states INTENT; the filesystem states FACT.** This
   file said `#194` r11 was "queued"; the worktree had six landed commits. Always
   reconcile `git log` / `git status` in the actual worktrees before triaging.
   Corollary: when writing entries, never say "r11" when you mean "the r11 review
   round" — that exact ambiguity misled a successor session.

5. **`scion resume <name> --force --non-interactive` restores the CONTAINER, not
   the WORK.** A resumed agent comes up with an empty prompt box and will report
   `STALLED (was working): Session started`. That is expected and is NOT a
   restore failure. **Resume is always: restore → send the dispatch → `scion
   look` to confirm.** Never one command. (Same delivery-vs-consumption gap that
   stalled `dev-xss-r4` at 12:53.)

6. **`orphan-scan.sh` cannot see uncommitted work or code commits.** Its safe-set
   is defined over `.design/project-log` commits only. A clean `unique_at_risk=0`
   from it says NOTHING about at-risk source changes. Do not use it as a
   pre-delete gate for anything but project-log loss until that gap is fixed.

7. **The preserve store lives INSIDE the population it protects.** All 85
   `refs/preserve/**` are in `/workspace/farmtable-em-verify195`; canonical has
   zero. Clones are also CHAINED (e.g. `farmtable-xss-r4`'s origin is
   `farmtable-xss-r2`, not a remote), so deleting a clone can break descendants.
   Nothing is pushed to GitHub. Preserve into CANONICAL, never into em-verify195.

8. **`scion delete`'s help claims it removes "associated files and worktrees."**
   Treat every delete as destructive to clone-only work. Preserve first,
   re-scan, and verify against a PRE-REGISTERED number — a preserve loop once
   reported 22 successes while fetching nothing.

9. **Security, open:** canonical's `git remote -v` prints a GitHub PAT in
   cleartext. Rotate + move to a credential helper.

## Periodic redraw investigation (task #144) - DONE, real root cause found, NOT a
## regression from today's changes
Investigation DONE 2026-07-24 19:13: PR #151. Two independent pre-existing bugs in the
GitHub passthrough polling path defeat Feature 55's upsert() equality check: (1)
passthrough.go set ClosedAt=time.Now() for closed GitHub issues (different every poll)
instead of GitHub's actual closedAt - fixed via a new GraphQL field. (2) task-store.ts's
JSON.stringify()-based equality check is key-order-sensitive, and remoteData (from a Go
map via structpb) has non-deterministic key ordering across polls - fixed with a
stableStringify() that sorts keys recursively. Well-reasoned root cause doc with clear
before/after flow traces. This is a genuinely old/pre-existing latent bug specific to
GitHub-sourced tasks, NOT a regression from today's Features 62-66/Perf work. Dispatched
`farmtable-periodic-redraw-review`, confirmed running - checking null-ClosedAt fallback,
stableStringify() correctness/perf, and whether other passthrough fields have the same
non-determinism class of issue.

## Auth Stage 4 pre-deploy fixes - reviewer caught a CRITICAL privilege-escalation bug in the rollout tool itself
`review-predeploy` reported REWORK 2026-07-26 23:36 on the EM's pre-deploy fix PR
(`auth-stage4-predeploy-fixes`, commits 381900a + 059f36c). Full report:
reports/review-predeploy-fixes.md. The StageTriage->StageBacklog pass-through fix (item 2
from the earlier gate) is CONFIRMED CORRECT, well-reasoned, minimal blast radius - reviewer
says it's safe to merge/deploy independently right now. But the NEW `ft token update` CLI
command the EM built AS the agent-token rollout mechanism (item 3 from the gate) has a
genuine CRITICAL bug: removing every scope from a token leaves the scope slice nil, and nil
is treated as wildcard (full admin) by the existing scope-resolution code - so
`--remove-scope` used to neuter a token can silently mint a full-admin token instead. Two
related High findings on the same command: `--add-scope` on a legacy wildcard token
silently demotes it to almost nothing, and `--remove-scope` on a `"*"`-scoped token is a
silent no-op that reports success. Zero test coverage on any of the new store/CLI code,
exactly where these bugs live. Real irony worth noting: the tool built to FIX the
over-privileged-token rollout problem would itself have introduced a worse privilege
escalation if used as-is.
Relayed to `farmtable-em-auth-implementation`: merge/deploy the pass-through fix
independently now if useful (reviewer-approved, separable), but do NOT use/ship the token
CLI command until C1/H1/H2 are fixed and covered by tests, with a required re-review
APPROVE before it's used for the actual rollout. Noted L1 (non-pass-through GitHub sync +
beads adapters still map to triage, same wall not yet addressed there) and M4 (no audit
log for scope changes) as follow-ups, not blocking. Acknowledged the reviewer's catch.

to fall back to at all - proto has zero token RPCs (no CreateAPIToken/ListAPITokens/
UpdateTokenScopes/RevokeAPIToken) and no CreateUser either, so direct SQL is not a stopgap
but the ONLY way to touch token/user data on Postgres today - makes I1's SQL guard-rail
warnings essential, not polish. (A2) `ft user` is split-brain: `create` writes local
SQLite while `get/list/whoami` read from prod over gRPC, so an operator who creates a user
then verifies with `ft user list` gets a false "not found" on the SAME CLI - a nasty trap
worth documenting explicitly. (A3) Root cause: `openDirectStore()` has no branch on
FARMTABLE_SERVER/--server (unlike `newClient()`, which does) - reviewer recommends (out of
#168's scope) a ~5-line hard-error guard there so future silent-wrong-results become loud
errors; flagged that whoever implements it must verify it doesn't break `ensureLocalUser`
or CI paths that intentionally set FARMTABLE_SERVER with embedded-mode semantics. Relayed
to the EM: proceed with the already-briefed C1/I1-I4 fix, file two SEPARATE follow-up
GitHub issues (openDirectStore guard; missing token/user management RPC surface) rather
than blocking #168 on either. No new blocking work added, just sharper context.

## Auth Stage 4 deploy prep - EM's rework introduced a NEW critical (dead-end pointer), caught pre-merge
`review-deploy-v2` sent a 2nd addendum 2026-07-27 00:13: the EM's C1/I1/I3/I4 rework landed
while the review was still open and is confirmed CORRECT for those four items, but
introduced a NEW critical (N1): the replacement text for step 3 (create the reviewer
identity) now points operators at "the server's gRPC API or the web dashboard" - NEITHER
EXISTS for this purpose. gRPC has zero user/token-creation RPCs (confirmed against the
proto). The dashboard's only creation path (OAuth auto-provisioning) hardcodes
Type=human and mints a 24h WILDCARD session token - the opposite of what step 3 needs.
Net: the runbook's own RECOMMENDED rollout route now has NO executable path on Postgres,
and a real operator would likely improvise by grabbing a wildcard OAuth token - exactly
the escalation this whole workstream exists to prevent. Reviewer proactively wrote the
fix: direct SQL user+token creation is fully feasible (HashToken is plain unsalted
SHA-256 hex, raw token format is deterministic) and provided a ready-to-paste bash+SQL
block. Key subtlety: on the SQL path, `type` is inert (DefaultScopesForUserType only runs
at CLI/provisioning time) - the `scopes` column is the only thing enforcement reads, so
`type='reviewer'` with no scopes silently means wildcard. Also N2 (doc references a
nonexistent `ft user delete` command) and N3 (unfilled GitHub-issue placeholder). Relayed
the ready-made fix directly to `farmtable-em-auth-implementation` with instructions to use
the reviewer's SQL block as-is, fix N2/N3, and get a final re-review before merge given how
many rounds this narrow doc fix has taken. Acknowledged the reviewer's thoroughness in
catching this before merge rather than after.

## Auth Stage 4 deploy prep - reviewer self-corrected: N1's SQL fix was schema-derived, not PG-verified
`review-deploy-v2` sent a 3rd addendum 2026-07-27 00:14, proactively correcting its own
earlier "ready-to-paste" claim: the N1 SQL block was verified against ent's migrate schema
+ a live SQLite dump, but NEVER executed against real Postgres (none reachable in the
review env). Two concrete PG-divergence risks flagged: (1) `gen_random_uuid()` needs PG13+
or the pgcrypto extension pre-13; (2) the `scopes` column is TypeJSON (maps to json/jsonb
on PG), so the bare string literal relies on an implicit cast - recommended explicit
`::jsonb` casts for robustness. Reviewer's own recommendation: run the block against the
existing PG integration test path (`server_postgres_test.go` + documented
`go test ./... -tags integration`) before treating it as verified - "five minutes converts
this from schema-derived to actually-verified, which is the bar this doc needs."
Relayed directly to `farmtable-em-auth-implementation`: do not ship N1's SQL as
copy-paste-ready until it's actually been run against real Postgres, not just SQLite.

   behind at /workspace/farmtable-task-state-web-ui was never actually a git worktree - a
   prior dev agent had run `git init` inside it after finding git broken (because a
   worktree's `.git` file points to a path that doesn't exist inside the container
   filesystem), producing a ROOT COMMIT with zero ancestry to origin/main - unmergeable.
   Root cause: scion's worktree-per-agent mode breaks inside containers because the
   worktree metadata path isn't valid there; agents "repair" by reinitializing git,
   destroying history. EM confirms this ALSO happened to `dev-task-state-predeploy-
   migration` and `dev-task-state-hotfix-179-r2` earlier in this exact workstream (their
   final states apparently still worked out via other means, but the pattern is real and
   has now hit 3 agents). Reconstructed the Phase 2 branch properly onto origin/main
   (content verified byte-identical to what reviewers actually reviewed) and switched to
   standalone git clones instead of worktrees for its remaining workspaces - confirmed
   this works correctly in-container. Endorsed adopting this as the project-wide default
   going forward given the recurrence.
3. GENUINE CONTRACT-READING CORRECTION: my brief said the toolbar's native-stage filter
   and kanban drag-to-change-stage were contract violations (inherited from the original
   test reviewer's finding). EM pushed back with the actual contract text (Section 10:
   "the native board should show stage lanes for triage, accepted, active stages, and
   terminal outcomes" - explicitly REQUIRES stage lanes; only "no native phase control" is
   banned). I verified this myself against the contract file directly - EM is right, my
   brief was wrong. The real, unambiguous violation is narrower: `ft-kanban-view.ts`
   writes `phase: newPhase` directly via `updateTask()` on drag - asserting a
   server-derived-only field from the client. Approved EM's recommended scope (A): keep
   stage filter/lanes/drag, ban only the phase write; added a refinement that a
   server-rejected drag (violating Phase 1's transition/accept/claim scope rules) should
   fail visibly (toast + snap-back) rather than silently. Two parallel devs now running
   (dev-p2-fixes for the 5 defects, dev-p2-tests for the missing component-level test
   coverage). Will run a full fresh independent review round (all 3 types) before merge.

## #189 follow-up: my "thoroughly tested" assumption was wrong - real gap found in live Phase 1
EM verified my ruling's premise rather than trusting it, per my explicit ask. Result: (A)
stands - confirmed unreachable today, all 4 availability implementations
(entstore.go/convert.go/multistore.go/passthrough.go) independently gate the full terminal
set. BUT my stated reasoning ("given how thoroughly that was tested") was WRONG - the
specific property (terminal stage -> Available:false) is asserted by ZERO Go tests despite
two test names that sound like they cover it (TestComputeAvailability_ReasonsAnd
TerminalDependencies has no terminal case in its table; TestComputeAvailability_
TerminalDependencyMatrix tests a different property - whether a terminal BLOCKER satisfies
a dependency, not whether a terminal TASK is available). Classic hollow-coverage pattern -
name implies coverage, table doesn't contain it - the exact same class of gap the round-3
mutation-testing pass was hired to find, just discovered sitting in ALREADY-SHIPPED,
3-review-round Phase 1 code instead. Also found: the terminal-stage check is duplicated
across 7 call sites, only 1 (isTerminalStage) is a named/exported predicate - a future 5th
terminal stage could desync 3 of 4 availability paths silently, reproducing #189 in exactly
the scenario my ruling says the client shouldn't guard against. Filed as #191 (table test +
consolidation onto the named predicate, test-only + mechanical refactor, no new behavior).
Noted symmetry: #190 (Phase 2 frontend BOARD_COLUMNS duplicating STAGE_LABEL) is the
identical defect class one layer up, already fixed in round 3.
DECISION: pulled #191 into this workstream but as its OWN separate PR (not bundled into
Phase 2's branch/deploy, since it touches live Phase 1 backend files and Phase 2 has
cleanly avoided touching Phase 1 so far - preserving that boundary). Same full review
rigor required despite being small, since it touches shared availability logic across 4
backend paths. EM to sequence based on capacity (parallel to Phase 2 fixes or right after).
Separate small deploy once merged, independent of Phase 2's eventual deploy. Good process
validation: asking an agent to verify rather than assume caught a real gap in
already-heavily-reviewed code - worth remembering next time something feels "surely already
covered."

tests are real. Zero Critical, zero in-diff High. All 3 independently flagged treewalk.go -
test-191's mutation M11 (predicate hardwired to false) left the ENTIRE
internal/platform/github suite passing - zero coverage, not just un-consolidated. EM
decided CONSOLIDATE over LEAVE with sound reasoning ("packaging is not concept" - treewalk
answers the same question as availability, just packages it as a readyResult instead of an
AvailabilityReason) - approved. EM added its own extra bar beyond what was asked: the new
exhaustiveness guard must be OBSERVED FAILING on a simulated new stage before being
accepted - a guard never seen to fail might not be a guard - approved, excellent instinct.
Also self-identified a SECOND instance of the exact same meta-pattern within this one PR:
test-191's own new test has a vacuous closing assertion (ClaimTask's rejection is actually
caused by an earlier PhaseClosed guard firing before computeAvailability is ever reached,
so the terminal-arm-specific assertion never exercises what it claims to) - fixing to pin
ErrAlreadyClosed instead. Approved.
TWO NEW REAL BUGS found in already-live Phase 1 GitHub-passthrough code, filed as #193/#194,
not blocking #191 itself: #193 (labels.go processes GitHub labels before real issue state
for closed issues, so an "accepted" label can forge available=true with an empty reason
list on a closed issue - currently only prevented by an incidental filter, not the terminal
predicate itself - a latent bypass, not yet exploited); #194 (CloseTask never swaps GitHub
stage labels the way UpdateTask/ClaimTask do, confirmed by EM checking there are only 2
production label-swap call sites and CloseTask isn't one - meaning the ORDINARY
claim-then-close lifecycle on GitHub-sourced tasks leaves a stale label and reports the
closed task as available, in production, today, no attacker needed).
DECISION: #194 gates Phase 2 (fixed as its own separate PR, same review rigor, small
dedicated deploy, sequenced before/alongside Phase 2's deploy rather than after) - reasoning:
Phase 2's new Available Queue is exactly the feature that would make this existing bug newly
and confusingly visible to users of GitHub-sourced collections, and it directly undermines
part of my earlier #189 ruling (server-availability-trust assumption holds for the core Ent
path but is demonstrably violated for GitHub passthrough in ordinary usage). #193 does not
gate anything - real and rightly filed HIGH, but only reachable via a filter-widening
change, not broken in ordinary usage today - tracked as normal-priority follow-up.
Notified ptone directly (heads-up, not permission-seeking) given #194 is a real live bug in
already-shipped code.

notifications were sub-agent-completion traps again (both still had live subagents

## Phase 2 R3 synthesis - held-for-all-3 discipline vindicated a 2nd time, new live vuln found
EM read all 3 reports: code REQUEST CHANGES (2 Important, already relayed), audit APPROVE
(0 Critical/High in-diff, but 1 MEDIUM that became #195, see below), test APPROVE WITH
FINDINGS carrying 2 HIGH SURVIVING-MUTANT findings absent from the code review entirely.
H-1: the id-tiebreak mutation (return 0) survived 362/362 green - both claimed-covering
tests defeated by sort stability since their fixtures already list tie participants in id
order. H-2: flipping reportRefusal's composed:true to false survived 362/362 - the
write-error event then never crosses the shadow-DOM boundary, so NO toast reaches the user
for ANY queue refusal, silently undoing the entire property an EARLIER round existed to
guarantee. Had the EM acted on the code review alone, both would have shipped open - 2nd
time this exact workstream's "wait for all three" discipline changed the actual merge
outcome, not just the paperwork.
HEADLINE CONVERGENCE: all 3 reviews independently landed on bandFor() from 3 different
mandates (I-1 correctness, a security MEDIUM, and the test-oracle finding) - correctly
ranked as the top r4 priority.
#189 REFINEMENT (not a reversal): auditor swept every availability consumer and found all
but bandFor are purely presentational - a hostile server gains nothing extra from the
ruling for display since it already controls the underlying data anyway. bandFor is
different in kind because availability there feeds a WRITE computation (rank arithmetic),
not rendering. Agreed: ruling stands, gets stronger once bandFor stops taking availability
as an input at all.
EM arbitrated a reviewer disagreement (code review said scope by !isClosedStage, audit said
drop the predicate entirely) - chose !isClosedStage with sound reasoning (terminal tasks
are dead weight since they never re-enter the queue; held/blocked/future-start tasks WILL
re-enter and need their rank preserved as an anchor) - nicely mirrors store.IsTerminalStage
from #191. Approved.
#194 SCOPE EXPANDED by the EM beyond what was asked: added a real ClosedAt arm to
ComputeAvailability (verified personally against actual GitHub state with an UpdatedAt
fallback so never nil, NOT label-derived) - fixes the actual invariant rather than patching
just the label-hygiene symptom, and gets partial #193 mitigation for free. Approved.
Sequenced dev-194-close-label-swap on top of #191's branch (terminal-predicate) specifically
to avoid a passthrough.go collision - smart. Merge order: #191 -> #194 -> Phase 2.
NEW LIVE VULNERABILITY FOUND, filed #195: audit's MEDIUM-1 - DOMPurify's default config
blocks script execution (verified against 29 payloads, 0 survivors) but does not strip
`<form action>`. GitHub issue bodies (arbitrary untrusted third-party content on any mirrored
repo) flow straight into Task.Description and render in the inspector - a working
page-replacing phishing form on the legitimate origin (target stripped, so submit REPLACES
the app rather than opening a tab, making it MORE convincing). Live in production today,
independent of Phase 2 shipping. EM correctly ruled it doesn't gate Phase 2 (Phase 2 doesn't
touch markdown rendering, so exposure is unchanged) but I overrode the "queue it as a 4th
PR shortly" framing - required it dispatched immediately in parallel with the other 3
running branches given how trivially exploitable it is (anyone who can open a GitHub issue)
and how cheap the fix is (2 lines). Notified ptone directly given this is the more
user-facing of the two live findings.
M-1 (attention view): EM settled on tracking as a known contract gap, explicitly not
claiming full Section 10 satisfaction in the completion report - agreed.
Status: dev-terminal-predicate-r2, dev-194-close-label-swap, dev-p2-fixes-r4 all running;
#195 fix dispatch requested to join them. review-191 re-review queued for when #191 lands.
#195 dispatched (dev-markdown-sanitize, base main independent of the #191->#194->Phase2
chain, can merge/deploy as soon as it clears review). EM found while scoping it that

reversed its own earlier M-1 call (see prior entry: "EM settled on tracking as a known
contract gap"). New position: CLOSE it, don't just track it. Grounds: (1) contract literally
says "attention VIEW for dependents blocked by unsuccessful terminal prerequisites" (line
638) - a card badge + inspector callout with no way to enumerate the set genuinely doesn't
satisfy "view"; (2) this isn't cosmetic - Section 11/line 664 ("cancelled and wont_fix do not
automatically unblock dependents") means dependents are PERMANENTLY STRANDED BY DESIGN, so
shipping the stranding semantics without a discovery mechanism is shipping half the design;
(3) the hard part already exists - attentionBlockers(task, store) is a real exported
predicate at task-state-utils.ts:186, already consumed by two components, so this is wiring
not a new feature. EM sequencing it AFTER r4 (not parallel) since an attention filter has to
touch task-filters.ts/ft-app.ts/ft-filter-chips.ts and ft-app.ts is exactly what r4 modifies
for the H-2 write-error fix - avoids a collision.
Also raised: (2) #194 is better framed as a contract violation, not just a bug - Section 14
acceptance criteria explicitly requires "ClaimTask rejects unavailable tasks by ID, including
triage, TERMINAL, held, dependency-blocked, and future-start tasks," making the earlier
gating decision independently contract-required, not just product judgment. (3) Phase
numbering is offset by one from the contract's own Section 13 numbering (contract Phase
1=review, 2=core data/API, 3=web UI, 4=docs) vs. this file's internal Phase 1/2/3 shorthand -
noted for accuracy, not reconciling the two conventions.
Per standing practice, independently verified both citations against the contract file
myself before ruling (did not take the EM's characterization on faith):
`grep -n -B2 -A5 "attention view|do not automatically unblock" design-task-state-model-contract.md`

per-task ComputeAvailability, so held/future-start/assigned-elsewhere/triage/terminal are

and tool outputs" under the contract's own vocabulary-survival checklist - this is

'ready' is retired vocabulary" as a contract ambiguity - checked the contract first, found

find-and-replace. Contract's own test is "must not survive as a SELECTABLE NATIVE VALUE,"
not "the English word must not appear" - blocked_by (relationship type),
BLOCKED_BY_DEPENDENCY (availability reason), and compat-only ON_HOLD are all legitimate

## CORRECTION 18:53-18:56 UTC - task #173 REOPENED, earlier "confirmed fixed" was premature
ptone flagged (18:51): "I don't see any active agents under the EM's supervision." Checked
directly rather than assuming this was benign:
- `scion list` showed all 4 dev agents apparently running again (recreated by the EM per my
  earlier instruction) - but `scion look` on all 3 I checked (dev-terminal-predicate-r2,
  dev-194-close-label-swap, dev-markdown-sanitize) showed the IDENTICAL fatal "Not logged in"
  failure, despite being freshly recreated minutes earlier.
- EM separately reported (18:53, before I'd even finished checking) the same finding with a
  much sharper root cause: recreated all 4, all 4 came up dead again, deleted them all again
  to stop notification noise. So "no active agents under EM" was CORRECT and expected - the
  EM correctly killed them once confirmed dead, not a separate bug or an EM lapse.
SHARPER ROOT CAUSE (EM's diagnosis, independently reproduced by me): the PROJECT-level
template registry is empty (`scion template status` still "No templates found") even though
`scion template list` shows all 16 templates exist fine at the GLOBAL/hub level. Because of
the empty project registry, `--type developer` resolution is A COIN FLIP - sometimes it
resolves to the real global template, sometimes it silently falls back to a DEGRADED config:
no `explicit_workspace:true` (mounts at PROJECT ROOT instead of the agent's own worktree
clone), `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL=haiku` instead of `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL=
haiku-4-5`, ~5 skills instead of ~24, no telemetry. The degraded config is exactly what lacks
auth provisioning.
I independently confirmed this by running TWO canaries with the identical command minutes
apart: canary 1 (the one I reported earlier as "fix confirmed") mounted correctly at its own
worktree clone and authenticated fine - a lucky draw, not proof the system was fixed. Canary
2 (run specifically to double-check after ptone's message) mounted at the PROJECT ROOT
(degraded signature) and failed identically to the EM's dead agents. Same command, same
minute-scale window, opposite outcomes - conclusively template-resolution flakiness, not a
one-time incident that resolved.
SECONDARY COMPOUNDING ISSUE (EM's finding): the hub agent-creation endpoint itself
(`POST /api/v1/projects/<id>/agents`) returned "context deadline exceeded" on 5 of 7 attempts
during the EM's recreation attempts - a second, independent path to a template-less dead
agent (times out mid-creation, phase=created with no container, finishing with a bare
`scion start <name>` with no --type produces zero-template container).
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS: owned the mistake explicitly to both the EM and ptone rather than
quietly revising - told the EM directly "that was my error, sorry for the false all-clear."
Told the EM to stand down from further retries (each attempt is a coin flip burning calls
against an already-flaky endpoint) rather than resume-instruct again. Declined the EM's
workaround offer (I create agents, EM drives by message) since my own creation path is
exactly as unreliable, not a stable channel to route around the real problem. Sent ptone a
corrected, sharper writeup (reports/2026-07-27-infra-blocker-container-auth-UPDATE.md) laying
out the exact registry/resolution mechanism and the compounding endpoint-flakiness issue.
Reopened task #173 (renamed to reflect "intermittent, not resolved").
LESSON FOR FUTURE INCIDENTS: one successful sample is not sufficient evidence an intermittent
infra issue is fixed, especially when the failure mode is exactly "sometimes resolves
correctly, sometimes doesn't" - should have run several consecutive creations before
declaring victory and lifting the freeze. Applying that bar now: will need multiple clean
creations in a row before calling this fixed next time, not one.
STATUS: holding again. EM standing down, worktrees/briefs intact, six review containers
untouched. Awaiting either ptone's fix confirmation (this time verified properly) or further
diagnosis.

## TRUE FINAL RESOLUTION 19:32-19:33 UTC - task #173 CLOSED for real, endpoint theory retracted
EM ruled out my endpoint-divergence theory cleanly from its own raw logs: its FAILING runs
showed the identical "deprecated endpoint /groves/..." debug line I'd keyed on - same
projectID, same CLI commit (68b8a3b1) as mine. That line is a pre-flight GET lookup, not the
create call; the actual create POST goes to /projects/<id>/agents for both of us. No endpoint
distinction, no CLI difference existed. Retracted my theory to the EM immediately (third
theory this incident that didn't survive contact with better evidence: registry, then
endpoint, both wrong).
ACTUAL ROOT CAUSE (small, mundane, confirmed): `POST /api/v1/projects/<id>/agents` had a
transient bad window ~18:40-18:51 UTC - all 8 of the EM's templated creates timed out during
it. It recovered on its own by ~19:26-19:30 (my 2/2 and the EM's subsequent 4/4 both confirm
recovery). Templates, the project registry, and auth provisioning were never actually broken
at any point in this incident.
WHAT ACTUALLY MANUFACTURED THE "DEAD AGENTS": the EM's own retry method. When `--type`
timed out, it retried with a bare `scion start <name> "<task>"` (no --type). That succeeds
by definition, but a template-less create applies NO TEMPLATE BY DESIGN - no
explicit_workspace, minimal skills, mounts at project root, no template-provisioned auth.
That degraded profile is exactly what got diagnosed for hours as a platform auth outage. It
was self-inflicted by the retry method, not a platform break. EM stated this plainly and
apologized for the earlier "fleet-wide auth outage" framing rather than just quietly
reporting "fixed" - explicitly good, exactly the standard this project holds.
ACTIONABLE PLATFORM BUG (the one real, worth-fixing finding from the whole incident): bare
`scion start` with no `--type` silently produces a degraded, unauthenticated agent that
reports `Phase: running` and looks like a completely successful creation - no error, no
warning. This is what turned a ~10-minute endpoint blip into a multi-hour investigation,
since the natural retry-after-timeout is exactly the command that manufactures the bad
state. Recommended to ptone: refuse a create with no template, or warn loudly.
SMALLER GOTCHA relayed: `-w` takes a project-relative subdirectory, not a container-absolute
path (`-w /workspace/foo` -> fast clean 500 "workspace path does not exist"; `-w foo` works).
VERIFIED STATE (independently, not just relayed): all 4 dev agents recreated -
explicit_workspace=true, 24 skills, correct branches, zero fatal login lines. Spot-checked
`dev-p2-fixes-r4` myself via `scion look` - genuinely doing real work (362 tests passing,
working through its actual fix checklist: bandFor scoping, reorder guard, mutation kills,
vocabulary literal shadows). Not another false positive. `/workspace/farmtable` shared
checkout confirmed 0 modified files (no cross-contamination from the earlier degraded-mount
risk). Six review containers never touched, remain untouched.
NOT CLAIMED RESOLVED: restart-safety for previously-stopped agents is still UNVERIFIED - that
earlier test (resuming a stopped agent with known-good config, which also failed) happened
inside the bad window and has not been retested since recovery. Treating "resume" as unsafe
until re-verified; six review containers stay untouched on that basis, not just out of
caution.
ACTIONS: acknowledged the EM's correction and retracted my own theory to it directly, praised
the transparency (naming its own role rather than reporting "fixed" bare). Sent ptone the
final corrected writeup (reports/2026-07-27-infra-blocker-FINAL-RESOLUTION.md) with the real
root cause, the actionable platform bug, and the -w gotcha. Closed task #173 for real this
time - genuinely verified via 6 consecutive successful creations across two independent
actors (my 2, the EM's 4), not one lucky sample.

## NEW ESCALATION 20:03 UTC - HIGH process-fatal data race, GitHub #198 filed
audit-194 found (and review-194 independently converged on, its own M2) a real, demonstrated
`-race`-confirmed data race in internal/platform/github/passthrough.go: ensureLabelIndex
(:91-104) and ensureRepoID (:80-89) do unguarded nil-check-then-map-assignment, labelNameToID
(:106-109) reads the same map unguarded - no mutex on the struct, cached per-collection in
MultiStore.platforms and shared across concurrent gRPC requests. A concurrent map read/write
in Go is a FATAL unrecoverable runtime error - crashes the whole server process, not just the
triggering request, taking every tenant down. Two ordinary authenticated mutating RPCs against
the same GitHub-backed collection on a cold label index are enough (no special privilege) -
e.g. CreateTask+CloseTask, two CloseTasks, ClaimTask+UpdateTask. Predates d5db8c4, so present
in the currently-deployed Phase 1 binary.
EM explicitly named the one thing that determines urgency rather than guessing: whether any
GitHub pass-through collections are ACTUALLY in active concurrent use in production right now
("shipped is not reachable") - flagged this gap itself rather than repeating its earlier
mistake of relaying an alarming claim without checking the part that decides who acts.
ACTIONS: filed GitHub #198 (HIGH) with full technical detail, both auditors' convergence, and
the fix approach (RWMutex, self-contained, deliberately not folded into #194's PR). Dispatched
`farmtable-inv-github-collections-prod` (narrow, fast, read-only investigator - not a fix
task) to determine collection count/activity/concurrency evidence in production, per this
project's "delegate investigation, don't do it inline" discipline. Verified it started
cleanly (no auth issues, genuinely working) before going back to blocked. Awaiting its
bottom-line answer to decide hotfix-now vs normal-priority-follow-up.

## Pre-flight merge-train collision check - one real landmine found, resolved on the small
## branch - 20:36 UTC
EM ran a proactive collision measurement across the whole 4-branch merge train
(#191/#194/#195/Phase2) rather than waiting for rebase time to discover problems, since Phase
2 was reviewed against 7a0f220 but 3 branches land ahead of it and nobody had actually
measured what that would hit. Findings: #191<->#194 already handled (rebase onto d7314cf,
same file). #191/#194<->Phase2: NO overlap, Phase 2 touches 0 .go files. #195<->Phase2:
overlap in package.json/package-lock.json/tsconfig.test.json.
Two of three self-resolve cleanly, with real credit given: tsconfig.test.json's
`src/**/*.test.ts` glob subsumes #195's explicit include, and Phase 2's new
run-node-tests.mjs globs test files rather than hardcoding a list AND hard-fails on a
source/compiled file-count mismatch - its own docstring anticipates "files that arrive from
other branches at merge time." Without that design, resolving the conflict in Phase 2's favor
(the natural default) would have silently stopped running #195's sanitizer tests - green
build, zero sanitizer coverage, no signal that anything was missing.
THE ONE REAL LANDMINE: #195 declares jsdom@^29.1.1 (markdown.test.ts uses it directly to give
DOMPurify a real DOM), Phase 2 declares jsdom@^26.1.0 (vitest environment for its 407-test
harness). >=26<27 and >=29<30 are disjoint ranges - npm installs exactly one, so whichever
branch's version loses runs its suite on an untested jsdom major. Verified the Phase 2 side
myself directly: `git show task-state-web-ui-v2:web/package.json` confirms jsdom ^26.1.0 at
head 633f8f2, matching exactly. Couldn't check #195's side (private worktree, consistent with
every other cross-worktree verification this session) but accepted on the same
specificity-and-consistency basis as prior EM claims.
EM'S CALL, AGREED: settle the version on the SMALL branch (#195, 6 files) rather than let it
surface mid-rebase of Phase 2's 73 files, where a security-relevant dependency judgment would
get made mechanically by whoever's resolving the rebase, likely without anyone registering
what was actually decided. Added to the #195 cleanup brief as an empirical task: test whether
the sanitizer suite passes on jsdom^26 - if yes, adopt it and the conflict evaporates; if no,
keep ^29 and document the failure (a jsdom-version-sensitive sanitizer would itself be a real,
worth-knowing fact about a security-critical test). EM explicitly told the dev not to force
either direction. Recorded in the deploy plan, flagged to Phase 2 reviewers as tracked context
rather than a finding against them.
GENERALIZABLE LESSON, worth keeping beyond this workstream: review approves a branch against
the base it was written on, not against the merge - a multi-branch train needs its collision
surface measured before the first merge lands, not discovered by whoever ends up doing the
rebase under pressure.
ACTIONS: verified the reachable half of the technical claim myself, agreed fully with the
resolution approach and the small-branch-first reasoning, praised the credit-where-due catch
on the Phase 2 author's forward-compatible tooling design. No coordinator decision required -
EM only flagged in case of disagreement, and there is none.

## TWO SELF-CAUGHT DEFECTS SURFACED BY THE RESTART - one of them the sharpest lesson of the
## entire workstream
1. `-w` IS A HOST PATH, not a container path - `-w /workspace/farmtable-markdown-sanitize`
   fails with "workspace path does not exist" (broker resolves host-side); correct form is
   `-w farmtable-markdown-sanitize`. EM realized this explains the two earlier "scion start
   printed help" events previously logged as a transient CLI quirk - the real error prints at
   the HEAD of output, above the usage dump, and was being silently discarded by piping
   through `tail`. SELF-APPLIED LESSON: I (coordinator) have been piping scion output through
   `tail -N` all session for readability - if a real error prints before a usage block, I've
   been discarding exactly the diagnostic information that would explain a failure, the same
   way the EM's own pipeline did. Adjusting practice: check full untrimmed output whenever a
   `tail`ed result looks like bare usage/help text with no clear error, rather than defaulting
   to "known transient Hub timeout" (which has been sitting as an unexamined assumption in
   this file for hours).
2. THE SHARPEST LESSON OF THE WORKSTREAM: three review clones were created via `git clone
   --shared`, so `.git/objects/info/alternates` pointed at a host path
   (`/workspace/farmtable/.git/objects`) that doesn't exist inside the container.
   `audit-phase2` failed LOUDLY ("unable to normalize alternate object path") - fine, visible,
   safe. `review-phase2` did NOT fail visibly - it silently ROUTED AROUND the damage by
   cloning to `/tmp/ftrepo` and fetching the branch from origin instead, which was 17 commits
   behind (6c0fcfb vs 633f8f2) - missing precisely the r4 fixes and the entire attention view,
   i.e. the whole delta the review exists to cover. It would have completed, produced a
   verdict, and READ AS A LEGITIMATE REVIEW while covering a tree with none of the actual
   changes - nothing in the report would have shown this. EM caught it only because the
   `/tmp` workaround looked odd and it went and checked what origin's head actually was rather
   than trusting a review that completed without complaint.
   GENERALIZABLE PRINCIPLE, stated by the EM and worth treating as standing policy: "a broken
   environment does not reliably produce a broken-looking result. An agent capable enough to
   route around infrastructure damage will silently convert an INFRASTRUCTURE failure into a
   CORRECTNESS failure and hand back something shaped like success." This is harder to catch
   than a failure that announces itself, because it doesn't announce itself as a failure at
   all - it announces itself as success. NEW STANDING RULE proposed and adopted: any agent
   that silently reroutes around missing infrastructure (fetches origin instead of its
   assigned clone, works in /tmp instead of its worktree, etc.) needs its actual working state
   checked before its output is trusted, regardless of a clean completion report.
   Fixed properly: stopped all three, ran `git repack -a -d`, removed the alternates,
   verified each clone standalone/fsck-clean, verified `7a0f220..633f8f2` resolves to the
   correct 73 files/39 commits. Restarted with explicit guards: do not clone elsewhere, do not
   fetch origin, do not work in /tmp, verify branch+head+commit-range before starting.
   Also noted: the canary I'd asked the EM to run (dev-195-cleanup) happened to be the ONE
   workspace built correctly (standalone full clone, not the shared-clone pattern that broke
   the three review clones) - "a single canary validated the fix and told me nothing about my
   own broken prep." Reinforces: one success proves the specific thing tested, not everything
   adjacent to it.
ACTIONS: acknowledged both defects explicitly, treating the alternates/silent-reroute one as
the sharpest finding of the whole workstream (sharper than the earlier phishing-payload
near-miss) and adopting the generalizable rule myself. Acknowledged the tail-masking issue as
a real catch on MY OWN practice, not just the EM's, and committed to checking full output when
a tailed result looks like bare usage/help with no clear error.

## FIRST REAL FINDING FROM THE RESTARTED #195 CLEANUP - <svg><style> sanitizer bypass

in `dist/purify.cjs.js` before ruling, rather than taking the dev's report on faith. RULED:
add 'style' to FORBID_TAGS this commit - it's strictly more capable than the two things
already scoped (`<dialog>`, class-reuse), so forbidding the weaker two while shipping the

## EM's OWN near-miss disclosed - same shape as mine an hour earlier, self-caught - 00:02 UTC
EM ran `scion delete dev-phase2-fixes-r5` BEFORE verifying the clone was safe. That clone held
the ONLY copy of the entire Phase 2 line - 9 commits on no remote, including the full §10
attention view and the whole r5 fix round. It survived (deletion didn't take the worktree
this time) - by luck, not by correct process. EM disclosed this plainly rather than quietly
fixing and moving on.
ROOT CAUSE, correctly generalized: the EM's own standing rule ("never delete agents with
uncommitted work") technically held - the work WAS committed, the report WAS written outside
the clone - but the rule was too narrow. The actual dangerous state isn't DIRTY, it's
COMMITTED AND UNPUSHED. `git status` clean can still mean "the only copy of this is about to
be destroyed." This is EXACTLY the shape of my own near-miss an hour earlier (the cleanup
instruction for the two parked agents) - the EM explicitly named the humbling parallel:
catching a hazard once doesn't inoculate you against walking into the same shape an hour
later. CORRECTED RULE: run `git log --branches --not --remotes` before any `scion delete`,
not just `git status`.
DURABLE FIX, not just a note-to-self: created git bundles of all three at-risk branches in
the scratchpad (attention-view bcd40a4/9 commits, close-label-swap 9f98ad8/13, markdown-
sanitize 5daace4/5 - all zero remote refs), named by branch AND SHA. Chose BUNDLES over
pushing to remote deliberately: pushing unreviewed work to preserve it would trade a

## #194 GATE FAILED - real security regression found, coordinator ruling made - 00:26-00:28 UTC
Both #194 round-2 legs independently REQUEST CHANGES, no split, both arriving by measurement

authz gate computes required scope from `existing.Stage`; the terminal-stage rule requires

cancelled issue back into the active pipeline - exactly the class of laundering the system
already defends against for the analogous triage case, reopened here via a different
mechanism (rewriting the source field instead of the destination check).

it's the identical bug via the real mechanism. NET: audit right about risk/wrong about
mechanism, test right about mechanism/wrong about severity - accepting EITHER report as

## Code-reviewer blocker fully root-caused - precise skew mechanism + the night's final,
## rarest lesson - 00:52 UTC
EM diagnosed the exact mechanism while blocked, and disclosed catching its own wrong first
conclusion before sending it. Root commit: 2f5952da5177 (2026-07-27 23:42 UTC, "consolidate
review methodology into a single code-review skill") renamed skills/pr-code-review to
skills/code-review AND updated the code-reviewer template's scion-agent.yaml atomically in
the SAME commit - the repo was consistent before and after, explaining why the leg worked
earlier tonight and broke about an hour in, not from the start.
EM's FIRST CONCLUSION WAS WRONG, caught before sending: initially read this as "not a cache,
template has a stale reference, one-line repo fix needed" - would have redirected ptone away
from the actual fix. Checked one more time and found the template was already correctly
updated in the same atomic commit - nothing in git needs changing.
ACTUAL MECHANISM: a version SKEW, not plain staleness. The broker holds a CACHED template
manifest from BEFORE 23:42 (still naming pr-code-review) and resolves it against a FRESH
repo ref from after the rename. Stale-manifest+stale-ref would work; fresh+fresh would work;
ONLY the mixed pair fails - meaning the broker refreshes the repo ref independently of the
cached manifest that named the skill, which will break on every atomic rename elsewhere too.
FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION TESTED: if right, blast radius = exactly one template (2f5952da5177
touched only code-reviewer's files). Confirmed against data already in hand: test-engineer/
security-auditor/developer worked fine ALL NIGHT, only code-reviewer ever failed - matches
exactly.
ACTIONS: escalated the precise diagnosis to ptone, explicitly distinguishing two different
fixes - (1) invalidate the broker's cached code-reviewer manifest (fixes it now) vs (2) stop
the ref and manifest refreshing independently of each other (fixes the actual bug, prevents
recurrence on the next atomic skill rename anywhere) - recommended both, not just #1.
THE NIGHT'S FINAL AND RAREST LESSON, explicitly framed by the EM as the MIRROR of the earlier
one: the earlier rule was "when a measurement conveniently confirms your fear, distrust it"
(the false-positive bundle-restore incident). This is the OPPOSITE temptation: a diagnosis
that flatteringly made the EM the lone clear-eyed observer (everyone chasing a cache, but
actually it's just an unnoticed rename) - MORE seductive than fear-confirmation, because
being right feels like diligence rather than a warning sign. It survived one step of evidence
and died on the second. GENERALIZED: "a diagnosis that makes you the lone clear-eyed observer
deserves the same skepticism as one that confirms your fear" - and the discipline is
identical in both directions: take the second measurement before sending, regardless of
which way the first answer flatters you.
ACKNOWLEDGED IN FULL: this closes tonight's identifier/measurement theme (6-7 instances of
"an identifier implied continuity that only measurement established") with a DIFFERENT axis
entirely - not about what you check, but about WHY you stop checking. Fear-confirmation
announces itself as unpleasant; this announces itself as competence, which is what makes it
more dangerous. Praised the falsifiable-prediction methodology on its own merits too - not
just a plausible mechanism, but a specific checkable consequence (narrow blast radius)
confirmed against pre-existing observations, which is what makes it a diagnosis rather than a
story.

### #194 @ 651da26 - REQUEST CHANGES, 2 High
Legs DISAGREED ON FACT, not just verdict: test-194-r3 (26KB, excellent, arrived first) wrote
"tried hard to break it and could not." audit-194-r3 produced a working PoC that defeats it.
EM ran the PoC itself: 12 of 16 authorization bypasses succeed, plus a scheduling bypass. Had
EM trusted only the (excellent, first-arriving, wrong) test report, it would have merged a
bypassable authz fix - the exact failure this whole gate exists to prevent, now realized, not
hypothetical.
SHAPE OF THE NEAR-MISS: the audit leg that found the truth initially wrote NO DELIVERABLE AT
ALL - caught only because EM checked the reports directory rather than trusting a completion
signal, and SALVAGED the audit's uncommitted PoC. The test leg that missed the bug offered to
"re-approve on inspection of the diff without another full round" - a shortcut that would have
shipped the bypass. Neither leg alone produces the right outcome; the audit's own deliverable
existed only because the EM went looking beyond the signal.
ROOT CAUSE: TerminalLabelStage (the entire basis of round 3's fix) is built on
MapLabelsToStage, which collapses a label SET to one highest-precedence winner, and
stagePrecedence ranks every non-terminal stage above every terminal one - so
`ft:stage/accepted` next to `ft:stage/wont_fix` on the same issue returns exactly the value
the fix was built to avoid.
THE MEASUREMENT NEITHER LEG MADE: EM measured the bug across 3 points in history (pre-F2,
post-F2, round-3) rather than assuming continuity - found the MULTI-LABEL bypass PREDATES F2
entirely; round 3 restored exactly the ONE cell F2 broke and no more.
THE GENERALIZABLE INSIGHT, elevated to a standing principle: "restore pre-F2 behaviour" has
been the operating remediation target for THREE ROUNDS and is NOT a sufficient specification
of done, because pre-F2 was already wrong in the neighboring cell. A restore-shaped target can
only recover the diff someone noticed - it structurally cannot find a hole that was always
there. Target rewritten positively: "authorization must never read a precedence-collapsed
label projection." ADOPTED BY THE COORDINATOR TOO: phrase future rulings as "state the
invariant violated," not "undo the regression" - the regression-framing quietly assumes
everything before the regression was correct.
FOURTH INSTANCE of "a check that derives from the thing it is checking cannot falsify it":
the dev rejected NativeLabel in round 3 for exactly this reason, then built TerminalLabelStage
on MapLabelsToStage - the identical structural error one level down, in the SAME round it named
the class correctly. Recognizing an anti-pattern doesn't grant immunity to your own instance
of it.
EM'S OWN NEAR-MISS ON ITS OWN MEASUREMENT: first run of the pre/post-F2 table returned
identical "accepted" for all 5 label sets - `LabelConfig{}` had left the mapper disabled.
Caught on the UNIFORMITY (5 different inputs -> 1 identical output is itself a tell), same
false-positive shape as the earlier restore-checker bug. Filed as a standing bar.
dev-194-fixes-4 dispatched with the rewritten positive-specification brief.

match. Dev considered 3 closures, correctly took none: banning .prototype assignment (spelling
with unbounded equivalents - defineProperty/Object.assign/Reflect/setPrototypeOf/__proto__ -
fakes coverage); freezing globals (production code change, out of scope); a runtime canary
that re-asserts the sanitizer's actual EFFECT against a live payload (the real answer - kills
V23/V25/unforeseen siblings regardless of spelling, since it checks effect not syntax).
EM DID NOT ASSIGN THE CANARY, with 3 explicit weighted reasons: (1) it IS the substance of
Phase-2's already-planned component harness - building it twice would be exactly the
shared-infrastructure duplication the EM is meant to prevent; routed to its own task #9 with

runner with hand-installed DOM, real risk to an otherwise-clean gate at round 5 with zero

THAN ASSERTING IT: the one V25 variant a static rule can never reach is an ACCIDENTAL
third-party prototype-patcher (Zone.js-style, no malice, real ecosystem pattern) - a genuinely
real class and the strongest argument for doing the canary now. Verified NOT live for the
actual dependency set (lit/shoelace/dagre/grpc-web/protobufjs/dompurify/marked - none are
known prototype patchers). Self-aware framing: "I went and looked because the convenient
answer here was 'out of scope, stop,' and that is the answer I should trust least" - a further
generalization of tonight's epistemic thread, this time distrusting a CONCLUSION that
conveniently ends the work, not just a measurement that conveniently confirms a fear or a
flattering theory.
NEW CLASS 2, a critique of the EM's OWN TOOLING from 2 rounds ago: the exit criterion ("no
mutation of the 2 REQUIRED_SINKS files can leave them unsanitized while green") never named an
adversary - read literally it demands surviving an attacker who can already run arbitrary code
in the guarded file, and that same adversary could edit the guard too, so the criterion was
UNSATISFIABLE from the moment it was written, not just incomplete. It still did real work
(correctly classified V23 as blocking, exactly the call it was designed for) but could never
have signalled when to stop, which was its entire purpose. AMENDED with an explicit,
honestly-scoped threat model: defends against innocent-looking regression at the two sinks
(aliasing/shadowing/re-homing/rebinding/argument-shape drift/unscanned-file laundering/
sanitizer-config capture); does NOT defend against a committer who can already land arbitrary
code - that adversary is code review, CSP, and Trusted Types. GENERAL PRINCIPLE STATED, judged
to travel beyond this case: "rules of this kind can own a name. They cannot own an effect."
V23 was closable because the attack had to name something and R8 could own that name; V25
names nothing - not a gap in the rule, the actual boundary of the technique.
PROCESS INTEGRITY NOTED: "the dev met the criterion I should have written, and reported
honestly that it did not meet the one I did write" rather than reinterpreting the flawed
literal criterion favorably to claim success - the costly, trustworthy form of disclosure, not
the free kind.

## Transport corruption is SELECTIVE, not uniform - the sharper finding, and a hard rule
## adopted with no exceptions - 02:05 UTC
EM caught a SECOND corrupted message from me (the one describing the fix itself, sent via a
plain double-quoted argument before I'd switched to the file-based method - reverted to the
unsafe path out of habit while narrating the safe one). Provided the sharper analytical point
unprompted: the corruption in BOTH instances was not random - it specifically and only
destroyed spans containing shell metacharacters, which in a technical coordination channel
are disproportionately the highest-value content (identifiers, exact commands, code) relative
to surrounding prose. "A loss channel biased toward destroying precisely the parts of a
message most worth sending." Worse than uniform loss in a specific way: degrades gracefully
in appearance while degrading catastrophically in content - a message missing its one command
example still reads as a competent summary. Both instances were only caught because the
deleted span happened to leave a syntactic hole (double space, dangling article); a backticked
clause between two commas, or an adjective phrase, would vanish into a fluent sentence with
the wrong meaning and no detectable seam.
CONSEQUENCE: proofreading/rereading sent messages cannot be relied on as a defense, since
detection depends on lucky syntactic tells that won't always occur. THE FIX MUST BE
STRUCTURAL: route ANY message containing backticks or dollar-parens through a file + quoted
heredoc, unconditionally, every time - not a preference to remember, a hard rule with no
exceptions, precisely because the earlier "adopt this going forward" resolution was itself
violated once, immediately, out of habit.
Appended to the taxonomy as its own line, sharper than the original: not just a transport
that delivers something nobody wrote, but one whose losses are correlated with the value of
what was lost.
STATUS: unchanged - holding on all six agents. No infra blockers, gate remains three legs.

falsification charges). The EM corrected me: only the #194 catch came from a
charge; the #195 arity catch came from the *developer's* own independent
discipline (chose to test the premise instead of implementing it) — no charge
existed for it. EM named my conflation explicitly as the same error-class it has
been tracking all night (generalizing from one instance to "the mechanism").
Accepted the correction without pushback.

EM's sharper point: a hand-picked charge only fires on a claim already recognized
as worth charging — both of its actual errors were in sentences confident enough
not to be flagged. That is a structural blind spot in targeting, not a vigilance
failure. Proposed fix (my first read): a standing brief-wide clause — "every
load-bearing claim in this brief is unverified until you verify it, finding one
false is a finding" — to close the gap independent of correctly guessing risk in
advance.

EM's second correction (same exchange, one message later): I mis-restated this as
"replace hand-picked charges with a blanket one." EM: **additive, not replacing**.
Targeted charges are what produced the arity and label-cardinality catches by
directing effort at a specific suspicion; a blanket clause could not have
generated either finding on its own — it doesn't know where to look. The two
mechanisms do different jobs: targeting directs effort to where yield is expected;
the standing clause covers being wrong about where that was, including wrong about
one's own sentences. Both being kept.

EM's own guard against the new clause going decorative: keep it short, placed
where unmissable, concrete about reward (a false claim = a filed finding, not a
courtesy note). Self-imposed check: if two rounds pass with zero findings filed
under that clause, treat that as evidence the clause is decorative, not as a clean
bill of health — re-examine rather than assume.

Net: two small real coordinator errors (both conflations of "which mechanism did
this") caught and corrected by the EM in real time, both accepted plainly. No
decision was required of me in either case — EM flagged, self-corrected, and
proceeded. Still holding on all six review legs (three for #194 round 5 at
`ea8ac39`; three for #195 round 6 at `86f30bc`). No merges until all three legs of

## 2026-07-28 04:09 — A defect that lived in the seam between two legs (new failure class)

#194 round 6 ran two parallel legs by disjoint ownership: Leg A owns
`internal/platform/github/` (label mapper), Leg B owns `internal/server/` +
`internal/store/` (authorization gate). EM asked both, independently, whether
their two fixes met cleanly. Leg A: "complementary, no seam" (four-case walk,
all four correct). Leg B: **there IS a seam**, and Leg B is right.

`terminal_label_stages.go:120` builds `present := make(map[task.Stage]bool)`.
Two DISTINCT labels resolving to the SAME stage collapse into one map entry.
Remove one of them and the resolved stage set is byte-identical, so
`SameStageSet` returns true, the gate in `server.go` short-circuits, and the
write is permitted on a bare `task:write` token — destroying a label nobody was
charged for. Leg A's premise (one-label-per-stage) held in all four cases it
walked but is not a property of the mechanism; its fixture could not construct
the two-labels-one-stage input, so the walk could not have found it. **Eighth
instance of "fixture cannot express the input"** — but this time the mechanism
producing the miss is organizational (domain partitioning), not a fixture
design choice. Keeping as a separate tag from the other seven despite the same
taxonomy label.

**The genuinely new part, EM's framing:** this defect was in NEITHER leg's
domain — it required the mapper's collapse AND the gate's short-circuit
simultaneously. Neither leg could have found it alone regardless of rigor,
because neither could see the other half. The boundary between two legs is
exactly the region no reviewer is assigned to during the round: each leg
reviews its own domain; the three-way only reviews the merged tree AFTER
combine. **The seam is unowned during the round itself.** A third failure mode,
distinct from "a leg is wrong" (independence) and "the brief is wrong"
(verify-before-asserting) — namely "the union of two correct domains is wrong,"
which no per-domain review structure catches by construction.

**Compounding detail:** Leg A's confident "no seam" was reached by verifying
against the EM's PROSE description of Leg B's change, not Leg B's actual diff —
agent containers cannot see each other's clones (every inter-clone git remote is
a dangling host path; `scion start -w` mounts a clone at `/workspace` inside its
own container only). So the combine question was answered against a summary,
not code. Same shape as the shared-brief-laundering finding from 03:43 — a leg
reasoning correctly over an input it structurally could not check — but this
time about inter-leg transport rather than a shared brief's premises.

**Two fixes, EM owns both:**
1. Publish every leg's diffs to `/scion-volumes/scratchpad` as they commit (the
   only cross-leg-visible transport that exists). Cross-leg claims must cite a
   diff, never the EM's prose.
2. The combine question is not delegable to either leg — EM adjudicates it
   personally, on a tree where both diffs are actually present.

**Routing:** the seam fix itself goes to round 7, not round 6 — it needs a
delta over LABELS rather than resolved stages, a contract change spanning both
domains while both legs are still mid-edit on them. Leg B lands a
characterization test asserting the CURRENT wrong behavior now, comment: "when
this goes RED the seam is closed, delete it." Deliberately not `t.Skip` — a
skipped test disappears instead of failing, already a named defect class here;
this way r7 cannot close the seam silently.

## 2026-07-28 05:29 — orphan-scan.sh built and run: entire #191 r2 review record was orphaned

Acting on the standing-verification instinct discussed earlier, EM built a
systematic tool rather than relying on catching near-misses by chance.

**Tool:** `/workspace/orphan-scan.sh`. SAFE = project-log commits reachable
from any canonical ref or any preserve ref; RISK = log commits reachable from
some agent clone, minus SAFE. Aborts on 0 preserve refs / 0 canonical commits
/ 0 clones scanned (fails closed, not open).

**Positive control, pre-registered before running:** `EXCLUDE_PRESERVE=1`
drops preserve refs from SAFE. Control run reported 41 at-risk INCLUDING a
known commit (`89306d0`), proving the detector can say AT RISK. Real run
reported 7, EXCLUDING `89306d0`, proving the preserve ref actually rescues a
commit rather than merely existing alongside it. The eventual "0 at-risk"
result means something only because the same harness demonstrably produced 41
under the control condition.

**What it found:** the ENTIRE #191 round-2 three-way review record (audit,
test, AND code review — all three legs) was orphaned, each surviving only
inside its own agent's clone on branch `terminal-predicate-r2`, reachable from
nothing canonical. **This task had already been marked COMPLETED.** The
reviews happened; the only proof they happened was one `rm -rf` from
permanently unrecoverable. Also found: the Phase 2 attention-view round-5 log,
and three Phase 1 commits, in the same state. All 7 now preserved and
ancestry-verified. 35 preserve refs total, 0 at-risk.

**Root cause, EM's own diagnosis, worth preserving verbatim:** "I treated
'agent reported COMPLETE and its report file exists' as sufficient to close a
round. The report file lives in the shared scratchpad; the project-log COMMIT
lives only in the agent's clone. Agent GC is then destructive. ptone's
instruction to delete agents promptly is right, but I was applying it without
the precondition it needs — 'confirmed done' has to include 'its commits are
reachable from somewhere durable.' Those two instructions were quietly in
tension and I did not notice until the detector made it visible."

**New standing rule:** `orphan-scan.sh` runs before any agent GC, every round.

**Second finding in the same exercise — a false-positive near-miss inside the
fix for the first one:** the preserve loop first ran under zsh, where
`$br:refs/...` triggered zsh's `:r` parameter modifier and silently corrupted
all seven refspecs. It failed loudly only because EM followed each fetch with
an explicit ancestry check instead of trusting exit status. Had it trusted
exit status, it would have recorded seven "successful" preservations that
never actually happened, with a correct-looking count — the identical shape
to the false-positive git-bundle lesson from earlier ("a false negative
announces itself, a false positive does not"), now at the git-refspec layer.
Void-artifact tally: 13.

**My own response — adopting the same precondition for my own practice, not
just endorsing the EM's:** my standing instruction (from CLAUDE.md) is to
delete agents once work is confirmed complete. I have been treating COMPLETED
status plus scratchpad report existence as that confirmation — the identical
gap the EM just named, one level up. Told the EM explicitly I'm adopting the
same precondition on my side going forward: before any agent gets deleted on
my authority, or before I log a phase as closed in this file, check
reachability from a durable ref, not just that a report file exists. This
applies session-wide, not just to the EM's own workstream.

Requested that `orphan-scan.sh`'s path and positive-control design get noted
in whatever closes out this workstream — it's infrastructure worth keeping
past tonight, not a one-off save.

EM went and measured for a recurrence of the DOMPurify inverted-ownership
pattern rather than treating the instance-level fix as closing the question,
and found one, unprompted, in the unrelated `#194` branch.

[MEASURED-BY-EM, read-only in the r7a clone, did not touch the combine
agent's tree]: 8 total paths reach a GitHub label mutation (6 via the shared
`writeLabelSwap` primitive, 2 raw `gql.addLabels`/`removeLabels` in

`RestrictLabelWriteToSnapshot` control has exactly 1 call site in the request
path: `server.go:840`, inside `UpdateTask` (handler at `:586`). Positive
control: the same grep shape finds 34 `FarmTableService` handlers, so it's
not a grep that finds nothing by construction. **One of eight — and the one
covered is the handler the original bug was reported against.**

**Structural identity with the DOMPurify case, not loose:** both have a
TERMINAL CHOKEPOINT every path must cross (`DOMPurify.sanitize` there, the
gql label mutation here), and in both cases the control got bound to A
CALLER instead of the chokepoint. There: the ownership guard bound to
`marked`, which runs upstream and is filtered by the thing left unowned.
Here: the narrowing bound to `req.AddLabels`/`RemoveLabels` in one handler,
protecting only the callers that were enumerated.

**Parent rule extracted, EM's own wording, worth keeping on the ledger as
the general principle rather than either instance:** "BIND A CONTROL TO THE
NARROWEST THING EVERY PATH MUST TRAVERSE. IF YOU BIND IT TO A CALLER, YOU
HAVE BOUGHT PROTECTION ONLY FOR THE CALLERS YOU ENUMERATED — AND THE
ENUMERATION WILL LOOK COMPLETE, BECAUSE THE CALLERS YOU WERE LOOKING AT ARE
ALL COVERED." Same animal as taxonomy form 8 (05:56 entry): there, the
fixture set derived from the pattern set, and full coverage of a closed list
read as completeness; here, the control's coverage derives from the caller
set the author was looking at, and full coverage of THAT reads as
completeness too. Form 8 = enumerations of patterns; this = enumerations of
call paths. Same failure surface; in both, the measurement everyone reports
(coverage) is exactly the measurement that cannot see the gap.

**Scope discipline, explicitly not overclaimed:** EM is NOT claiming seven
open bypasses — most of the other seven are independently gated elsewhere
(`CreateTask` by A-1; `ClaimTask`/`CloseTask` by their own scopes), per
r7a's 29-row table. EM's own new lead (`PriorityLabelSwap`/`TypeLabelSwap`
reaching `writeLabelSwap` ungated) is explicitly tagged

EM raised two items, one a calibration correction, one a question it explicitly
declined to answer itself (no production access) and routed through me.

**Calibration point (EM's, accepted without pushback):** A-4's threat model
was never an anonymous internet attacker — it's privilege escalation BETWEEN
AUTHENTICATED principals (someone already holding `task:write` escalating to
`task:close`-tier effects). IAP filters unauthenticated callers, which was
never in A-4's threat model to begin with. IAP genuinely lowers the ceiling,
but not for A-4 specifically — the population that can exploit A-4 is
approximately the population IAP admits. Not contesting ptone's "not urgent"
call; just don't want the writeup to claim IAP mitigates A-4 when the two
controls act on different axes.

**The question, and I measured it directly rather than relaying it as pure
text:** [MEASURED-BY-EM, `internal/server/scopes.go:74`]: `RequireScope` has
TWO fail-open paths — (1) `ctx.Value(authEnforcedKey) == nil` → allow
everything (open-access mode); (2) `len(scopes) == 0` → allow everything,
"nil/empty scopes = wildcard, backward compatible with existing tokens." Path
2 had not been flagged anywhere before tonight. EM's question: on the live
deployment, is auth actually enforced, and do the tokens in use carry
explicit scopes? EM explicitly declined to check itself (no production
access, standing instruction) and routed it as a question, not a finding.

**I checked both parts directly, since I'm not bound by that instruction:**

1. `gcloud run services describe farmtable --region=us-central1` — live env
   vars do NOT include `FARMTABLE_OPEN_ACCESS`. Confirmed against
   `main.go:66`'s exact check (`os.Getenv("FARMTABLE_OPEN_ACCESS") == "1"`).
   Matches the "Token authentication enabled (store-backed)" startup log line
   observed in production logs earlier tonight. **Fail-open path 1 is NOT
   active in production.**

2. Queried the live `api_tokens` table directly (same DB access used
   earlier). 3 rows:
   - `lifecycle-reviewer`: 6 explicit scopes
     (`task:read/write/claim/accept/close`, `collection:read`). Never used
     (`last_used_at` null).
   - `local-embedded`: `scopes` = NULL (empty). Never used.
   - `dashboard-env`: `scopes` = NULL (empty). **`last_used_at =
     2026-07-28T06:10:51Z`** — essentially the moment of this check, real
     ambient traffic, not anything I triggered (I only queried Postgres
     directly, never called the server's API).

**Conclusion — precise, split by credential, not a single global answer:**
fail-open path 2 (empty scopes = wildcard) IS real and IS being actively
exercised right now by `dashboard-env`, which appears to be the credential
backing live traffic. For requests under that token, every scope check in the
system — #194's new one and every pre-existing one — returns nil
unconditionally, by explicit backward-compatibility design, not a bug. For
requests under `lifecycle-reviewer`, the gate is fully armed. So the honest
framing is neither "A-4 was purely prospective" nor "A-4 was a real reachable

changes: `exploit=false`. Swapped the real gate in as oracle on the same
line: fired immediately. **THE INPUT SPACE WAS ADEQUATE. THE ORACLE WAS
NOT.** EM's remedy (widen the search axis) would have saved nobody.

**The real defect, better than EM's diagnosis:** the harness had hand-rolled
a PROXY ORACLE that reimplemented the function under test — per-label,
per-list. The real gate prices JOINTLY across both lists. A cross-list
defect is invisible to a per-label oracle regardless of input volume
("nineteen or nineteen thousand spellings, same result"). The
one-dimensional search was a SYMPTOM: spellings were the only thing the
proxy oracle could discriminate at all. **"The oracle silently defines the
reachable search space, and then saturation of that space gets mistaken for
coverage."** — the sharpest single sentence of the whole session.

**The self-referential twist, EM calls it the sharpest thing written on this
workstream:** the function's own docblock says "It is exactly the complement
of applyLabelDelta... the two must agree." The auditor quoted that docblock,
then built a verification oracle that independently REIMPLEMENTED the very
function the docblock said must agree with the real one. Auditor's own
words: "I committed inside my harness the identical error the code
committed. The bug and the audit that missed it have the same shape."

**Rule adopted:** when auditing a control whose contract is "mirrors F," the
oracle must BE F, never a reimplementation of F. With the real function as
oracle, a two-element input space catches the Critical. README and task #56
corrected.

### A standing bar known insufficient for the first time
"Positive-control-before-negative-claim" — the gold standard EM has run all
night — is NOT enough on its own. Both of the audit's positive controls
fired, but both were drawn from the OLD bug's axis (spelling) — i.e. from
inside the very oracle's blind spot, so they were never independent evidence
about axes the oracle couldn't see; they were just more samples from the one
axis it could. **New practice: draw controls from a DIFFERENT axis than the
one searched, or mutation-test the control itself.** My own framing sent
back to the EM: a same-axis positive control isn't weak evidence for the
failure that matters here, it's NON-evidence — a real amendment to the
standard, not a footnote.

from the orphan-scan class — not every loss from premature GC is a
data-loss risk; some is a capability-loss risk, and orphan-scan only catches
the first kind. A transcript of what a leg already said is not a substitute
for what it could still figure out if asked, because the answer to a
follow-up doesn't pre-exist anywhere waiting to be read — it has to be
produced by a live agent with intact context.

within my authority, not a product/architecture question):** adopted the

landed, and that kind of exchange can't be front-loaded into "ask everything
before adjudicating," because the adjudication process itself is often what
surfaces the next question — EM's own path to the oracle insight is proof:
it didn't know to ask about oracle design until after reasoning through the
(wrong) search-strategy explanation first. Front-loading assumes anticipating
what you don't yet know you'll need, the same failure shape as everything
else tonight.

materially over tonight's peak (19 agents / 57 clones) and a review leg's
fix has landed but not yet re-verified, GC it anyway rather than let
container count become its own risk. Buying the common case a longer window,
not treating extension as free. Told EM to flag if this tension actually
bites tonight for reconsideration.

Rule 14 says compare scanned-count to population; EM did that, with an
