glob, no matter what existed. Re-measured with an independent instrument
(`/workspace/*/`, sharing nothing with the filter): 177 dirs total, 174
matching the pattern, 3 not (downloads, shared-dirs, canonical farmtable
itself — deliberately the SAFE-set source). `find -maxdepth 3` for nested
`.git` outside the glob returns only canonical. **The glob was correct** —
but this is the SECOND time in an hour EM got the right answer from a check
that could not have contradicted it. EM's own conclusion, worth preserving
exactly: **"two right answers from a blind instrument aren't two successes,
they're one unexamined habit."** New rule 14a: the population must be
established by an instrument the filter does not share.

### S-3 — a positive control that passes via type confusion
`merge-verify.sh` picked its positive-control file with `head -1` on the
changed-file list — which may be an ADDITION, absent from BASE. Measured:
`git rev-parse "$BASE:<absent path>"` exits 128 and ECHOES THE ARGUMENT BACK
ON STDOUT. So the operand isn't empty (an `-z` guard wouldn't catch it
either) — it holds the literal string `"<sha>:<path>"`, which can never
equal a real blob SHA. The control then reports OK while comparing a blob
SHA against an error-echoed path string — always OK regardless of whether
the merge was actually correct. **A positive control that passes because its
operands are incomparable**, not because the comparison succeeded.

EM checked whether this had ALREADY manifested rather than assuming either
direction: the actual `merge-verify.out` log had picked a MODIFIED
project-log file (not an addition) and compared two real 40-char SHAs — it
did NOT fire; the earlier "MERGE VERIFIED" verdict stands untouched. Good
discipline: neither let a real bug stand unexamined, nor let it retroactively
poison a verdict it never actually touched.

Fixed with `--diff-filter=M`, `git rev-parse --verify --quiet || die`, and a
bare-hex assertion on both operands.

**Transmission detail, worth keeping as its own entry:** `merge-verify-r7.sh`
ALREADY had the `diff-filter=M` guard — EM had fixed this exact bug once
already, in a newer copy of the script, and left the OLDER broken copy on
disk, still runnable. EM's own framing: **"A superseded script that still
runs is not superseded."** Version drift between "the copy I remembered to
fix" and "the copy still on disk" is its own hazard, independent of whatever
bug prompted the original fix.

### S-2 (low), S-4 (clean negative, recorded on purpose)
S-2: `orphan-scan`'s own prerequisite guards had the identical `-d`/`.git`
twin bug — fail-closed, never a wrong answer, but made the tool unpointable

## 2026-07-28 08:05 — EM broke the #194 r8 round, legs caught it; dev-195-r9 verified; four new rules (22 is the sharpest of the night)

### THE FAILURE: host-path leak into guest clones, and an oracle-blind verification
All three `#194` r8 review legs reported their git object store EMPTY within
two minutes of launch. EM had created their clones with `git clone
--shared`, which writes a HOST path into `.git/objects/info/alternates`.
Each leg bind-mounts its clone at `/workspace`, so that path doesn't exist
in its own namespace. Every object-touching git command failed;
deliverable 2 (a committed project-log entry) was impossible.

**EM had verified those clones before launching** — HEAD, clean tree, assets
present, all green. It passed because EM ran the check FROM THE HOST, where
the alternate resolves. **"A check run on the host cannot falsify a defect
that exists only in the guest — the instrument shared the very property, a
host filesystem view, whose absence WAS the defect."** Oracle-blind-spot
pattern at yet another layer. EM's own rule 14 ("never put a host path in a
brief") did not fire because GIT wrote the path, not EM — the rule was
scoped to PROSE when the actual hazard is any host path in anything the leg
reads, tool-generated or not. Same shape as the `labelNamesToIDs` TrimSpace
gap: a rule true as far as its author thought to apply it, silently
narrower than the hazard.

**Epistemic note EM recorded deliberately, worth preserving exactly:** the
legs concluded "that directory no longer exists." That inference was
CORRECT from inside their namespace and FALSE about the world — the
directory is present from where EM sits. "Two containers, one filesystem,
two irreconcilable true beliefs, neither lying." EM explicitly told the legs
not to file it as their own error — a fair, correct call: blaming a correct
local inference for a shared-environment mismatch teaches the wrong lesson.

**Repair, structurally sound rather than just patched:** repacked and
deleted the alternates file — "with the file gone, any success proves the
objects are local" — same family as removing the docblock instead of
correcting it; don't leave a control standing that could pass by the same
accident twice. Swept all 180 workspace dirs with a NON-SHARED instrument
(avoiding repeating the exact same-instrument-shares-the-defect trap): zero
remaining, logged as a clean sweep per rule 18. Prediction miss recorded
honestly: predicted 2 pack files / tens of MB, got 3 / 2.2M.

- B3a's ordering rationale was not just false but CIRCULAR: "an early
  poisoner contaminates every later check" is only demonstrable on a tree
  where the check is ALREADY failing — the argument assumed what it needed
  to independently establish.
- EM relayed "two vacuous tripwires" when the true number was FIVE — the

### Four new rules
- **Rule 19** (mine, now operational): never invoke a principle to license
  destroying something — state the measurement showing it applies here, or
  ask the leg to measure first.
- **Rule 20**: the alternates incident, plus a four-item launch checklist.
- **Rule 21**, from the dev's best finding: **a fix can be class-shaped in
  the source and instance-shaped in effect, when a caller does the callees'
  work.** Round 8's five-scanner "class fix" had the caller pre-blinding
  once, so three of the five scanners were structurally UNREACHABLE — the
  fix was correct in isolation but its actual blast radius was smaller than
  its shape implied. Not a fixture problem, not an oracle problem — a fix
  whose correctness is real but whose reach can only be established by
  tracing actual callers, never by reading the diff.
- **Rule 22 — the sharpest formalization of the session:** "A LOOP IS
  NON-VACUOUS EXACTLY WHEN SOMETHING ASSERTS ITS RESULT FOR AN INPUT WHOSE
  ANSWER IS KNOWN IN ADVANCE." Five of six tree-wide loops were vacuous; the
  one red loop was the only one compared against a known count. Explicitly a
  DESIGN rule, not a testing rule — applies to any "for each X, check Y"
  construct regardless of whether it's ever called a test, and explains all
  five vacuous instances with one clean criterion instead of five separate

## 2026-07-28 08:08 — Rule 23: unstated scope of a defensive measure; a deliberately withheld finding preserving experimental integrity

EM tested my R14/TrimSpace generalization instead of banking it — "mostly
right with one real break."

### Underlying fact independently reconfirmed
EM had only held the `labelNamesToIDs` gap as `[MEASURED-BY-dev-194-r8]`;
confirmed directly: `passthrough.go:166` builds the index with `ToLower` and
no `TrimSpace`, `:201` reads it the same way.

### A sharper fact the dev never reported
`TrimSpace` IS used elsewhere in the SAME package —
`push_prefix_resolution_test.go` carries the comment "TrimSpace is
unicode-aware — verified, not assumed" and deliberately reasons about
U+200B not being whitespace. **This is not a team that failed to think about
whitespace folding — the same package normalizes carefully on one path and
by case alone on another.** Inconsistent normalization between two paths is
a STRONGER finding than a uniformly-missing one: the careful path proves the
hazard was understood somewhere, and the discipline simply didn't transfer.
"Nobody thought about it" has an easy fix (tell people); "someone thought
about it hard enough to reason about a specific unicode edge case, and it
didn't reach the next file" says correctness at one boundary doesn't
propagate to another by default.

### Rule 23 — what generalized, precisely scoped
The real shared core, now its own rule: **the SCOPE of a defensive measure
is itself an unchecked claim.** Nobody writes "this applies to X and not Y"
— the scope is implicit in the implementation, invisible to review.
Distinguished cleanly from form (8): form (8) is an enumeration whose
CONTENTS are incomplete; this is a rule whose DOMAIN is narrower than the
hazard, unstated.

### Where my analogy overreached — accepted and correctly limited
R14 had a REACHABLE, FINITE correct scope ("any artifact the leg reads") —
EM simply failed to write it down. Normalization has NO natural completion —
case, whitespace, NFC/NFKC, zero-width, homoglyphs, RTL is an open set with
no defensible stopping point. **A rule narrower than it should be, and a
rule that CANNOT be complete, fail differently and want different
remedies:** write the scope down (finite case) vs. pick a canonical form and
enforce it at ONE boundary (open-set case). "Add TrimSpace" is the tempting
fix here and the wrong one — it treats an open-set hazard as if completing a
checklist would close it, when the correct answer to an unbounded hazard is
a chokepoint, not a checklist.

### The discipline point — a live finding deliberately withheld mid-round
The inconsistent-normalization finding lands EXACTLY on the axis EM already
asked `audit-194-r8` to investigate independently (whether `ToLower` is the
right fold for a security-relevant identity comparison). **EM is
deliberately NOT relaying it while the round is open** — sending it now
would convert the audit's independent measurement into a confirmation
exercise, precisely what the three-way structure exists to prevent. Logged
as a held task with an explicit instruction not to relay, adjudication
logic spelled out IN ADVANCE: if the audit finds it independently, that's
genuine convergence, worth a great deal; if not, that's a coverage datum
about the audit (not a failure), and the finding still stands on EM's own
measurement regardless. Either branch produces information that relaying
early would have destroyed. Same pre-registration discipline EM has run all
night on numeric predictions, applied here to a qualitative finding instead.

### New taxonomy form proposed: the oracle's target moves after the oracle looks at it
`dev-prod-hardening` added a CSP with a `script-src` sha256 of the inline
theme script, guarded by a test recomputing the hash from the EMBEDDED
`web/dist/index.html`. `web/dist` is gitignored/untracked; a fresh clone
can't even `go build` without generating it first; nothing in `make test`
builds `dist`, and `make web` regenerates it AFTER the last Go test run.
**Measured, predictions recorded first, both confirmed:** edit the inline
script in SOURCE, don't rebuild, run the guard → GREEN (stale pass).
Rebuild, re-run → RED with the correct hash (guard IS non-vacuous, given
the right dist). But the guard still cannot falsify the actual shipped
artifact: edit source → `make test` green against stale `dist` → `make web`
rebuilds with the new script → `make build` embeds the new `dist` but with
the OLD hash baked into the CSP header → **browser silently blocks the
newly-updated legitimate script.**

EM's framing: "the check does not derive from the thing it checks, it
derives from a STALE COPY of it" — asked for my judgment on whether this
deserves a new form rather than filing under (1). **My ruling: yes, name
it.** Form (1) and its relatives are about what a check CAN express at
check-time — a structural, permanent limit. This is about WHEN a check runs
relative to the surrounding pipeline — the check is fully capable of
expressing the right answer and does, but the artifact gets regenerated by
a LATER stage before shipping, so a true result at check-time becomes a
false guarantee by ship-time. Proposed name: **"the oracle's target moves
after the oracle looks at it."** Warrants its own number given the clean
two-arm demonstration with a pre-registered prediction, same standard
applied to rule 22.

### Rule 25 (the cross-branch-control rule) resolved as to mechanism, with a residual sting
The pre-registered must-ship-together position holds: `url-scheme-
validation` and `prod-hardening` have ZERO file overlap (Makefile supplies
invocation, `package.json` supplies content), neither alone delivers a
running scanner. `review-xss-r1` independently reached ship-together on its
own axis, unprompted — genuine convergence again. **Residual risk flagged
by EM:** `prod-hardening` deliberately omitted `npm ci` from its `web-test`
target to keep `make test` offline-runnable — well-reasoned in isolation,
and precisely what would hide the `tsc EXIT 2` Critical after the merge.
**Green `make test` will not imply green `make web` on the merged tree** —
flagged to be checked separately by whoever verifies the merge.

### New HIGH finding from dev-194-r9 — a durable write outliving the toggle it was gated by
My ruling had handed the dev leg a question with instructions to measure it
and STOP if open. **They measured it, found it open, and stopped —
exactly the intended behavior.** Finding: with `enabled=false`, the gate at
`server.go:840-860` prices NOTHING — a bare `task:write` holder can durably
write `ft:stage/completed`. Measured differential: `enabled=true` →
`PermissionDenied` requiring `task:close`; `enabled=false` → accepted,
label lands. **Then, after a LATER flip-on: `stages=[completed],
available=false`.** The label PERSISTS in GitHub, which never hears about
the internal toggle — flipping `enabled:true` later, "a config change
nobody would regard as a privilege grant," retroactively converts every
label written while disabled into an authoritative terminal state with NO
transition scope ever charged. Mirror image of MUST 5(b): config
correctness must not depend on a flippable toggle; this is a DURABLE WRITE
governed by the same toggle. Fail-closed doesn't save it —
`ErrEmptyLifecycleStageSet` never fires because with the mapper disabled
the gate is not REACHED, not reached-and-refused.

**My ruling, extending the earlier one rather than treating this as
separate:** the scope required to WRITE a lifecycle-prefixed label should
NEVER depend on `enabled`, regardless of what `enabled` means for reads. The
original ruling was about whether the system currently treats EXISTING
labels as authoritative for CURRENT permission decisions — a read-time/
authorization-derivation question, correctly gated by the toggle. A WRITE
creates durable state OUTSIDE the app, in GitHub, which never hears about
the toggle — so its future consequence is identical regardless of the
toggle at write-time, and gating the write by `enabled` just creates a free
window where privilege gets banked now and cashed out later on an unrelated
config change. **`server.go:840-860` should require the same scope for
lifecycle-prefixed label writes whether `enabled` is true or false — only
the read/authorization side should vary with the toggle, never the write
side.** Goes into r10 as a concrete instruction, not an open question.

### Rule 26 — filed correctly as a rule, not a form (my agreement)
"Overlapping oracle arms MASK each other": deleting P2's entire
cancelled-by-remove arm left the package at EXIT 0, because the broken
restrictor's output tripped two arms at once and the SURVIVING arm kept the
row failing — a multi-arm oracle read through a single bit is only as
strong as the UNION of its arms, so any arm whose triggering inputs are a
subset of another's can be deleted UNDETECTED. Remedy: return WHICH arm as
text, not a bool, with one row per arm and inputs that trip exactly one arm;
plus negative rows requiring SILENCE on correct output ("rule 22 applied to
an oracle instead of a loop"). EM filed as a RULE, not a form — nearest to
form (8) but inverted (the enumeration of ARMS is complete; the enumeration
of DISCRIMINATING INPUTS is not), and the remedy is a probe-construction
discipline, not a new way of being wrong. **Explicitly asked for my read —
I agreed without hedging:** the form list should stay restricted to genuine
failure axes; this is a "how do you verify a multi-part oracle actually
exercises all its parts" question sitting above the form list, same
restraint that correctly rejected form (9) earlier.

test probe** — the workstream's own defect class, arrived at from the
operational side.

SEAMS. Audit: an item list finds CONTROL WEAKNESSES while an open pass finds
PATHS — different blind spots, not the same finding restated twice, a
stronger argument for running both than either alone. **Audit pre-
registered a falsifiable prediction, mispredicted one of its own findings as
covered, and refused to edit the prediction afterward** — the discipline
that makes the whole experiment trustworthy. EM keeping the practice.

**One cost, self-charged correctly:** EM's dispatch message named item A2
in PROSE, so the leg read it before the baseline block — the §0 measurement
for that item is contaminated. Generalization: "the apparatus is every byte
the leg reads before §0, not just the brief file." Fix: a fixed, minimal
dispatch template (SHA, report path, "read the baseline block first,"
nothing else) — removes the surface for the mistake to recur rather than
relying on remembering not to editorialize.

### The five names and the bound

to probes whose killer set includes one of these five, not a general
"any test might flake" problem.

### Retroactive check: CLOSED, no re-opening

accepted matrices have a flaky name in the KILLER column — in ALL THREE the
flaky test was NOT the sole killer, and in all three the leg identified it
as a flake AT THE TIME (with re-run evidence, e.g. `test-194-r4`'s M4:

(`-skip TestWatchTasks`, or a tripwire grepping every RED for the name) or
was web-only (`#195` is npm-only, explicitly stated immune). **Conclusion:
no probe anywhere was counting on a flaky test to go red. Nothing already

### Self-applied form-6 flag on its own clean result
EM proactively qualified its own reassuring answer rather than let it stand
unexamined: the grep finds every row where a NAME was recorded, but cannot
see a row that recorded ONLY A COUNT (`test-194-r7`'s tables are
count-shaped, with names appearing only in adjacent prose) — "a form-6 risk
in my own answer... I would rather flag it than let the clean result stand
unqualified." Residual correctly bounded: any matrix after r7 excluded the
family by construction, so exposure is confined to r4-r7 era `#194`
matrices, all superseded by later rounds on the same code. Same rigor
applied to a good result as to a bad one.

### Durable, cross-cutting principle named: identity vs. count
EM: the retroactive question was answerable in ten minutes rather than
being the archaeology project I was right to want to avoid, because of a
rule already in force for an UNRELATED reason ("read failing test names,
never counts," adopted after a count once said 3 when the truth was 1).
**"RECORDING THE IDENTITY OF A RESULT RATHER THAN ITS COUNT IS WHAT MAKES A
RESULT RE-AUDITABLE AFTER ITS ASSUMPTIONS CHANGE."** Same shape as the
count-neutral ruling and X5 (file-count floor blind to which directories
were walked), now arriving from a THIRD direction — as a property of the
AUDIT TRAIL itself, not a gate. Added to `_BRIEF-RULES.md`.

**My extension, offered back:** identity subsumes count because it's
lossless with respect to it — a set of names can always produce a count on
demand, but a bare count can never produce the names back, and a record
that already threw away identity cannot recover it later no matter what's
learned afterward. Stated as the general rule: since you can never know in
advance whether a record will need to survive a change in assumptions
(you always might learn something new later), default to recording
identity. Also noted: a rule earning a second, unplanned use it wasn't
designed for is usually a sign it's pointing at something more general than
the bug that originally produced it.

EM also adopting my "trust a tool's self-report = trust a leg's own
approval, same failure at different layers" framing, writing it in with the
preserve-loop incident as its worked example.

## 2026-07-28 13:11 — Two scoping constraints on the GitHub-parity policy; a launch stall traced to EM's own delivery/consumption gap

### Constraint 1: the CSP dependency — may make it a prerequisite, not a parallel track
EM added, explicitly flagged as INFERENCE not measured fact: "GitHub has
proven this policy safe at scale" is true in GITHUB'S deployment context,
which includes compensating controls Farm Table demonstrably lacks — most
obviously NO CSP AT ALL on an origin holding a long-lived API token (task
#180/EM's #85, already measured tonight). An allow-list is a COMPONENT of a
defense posture, not a standalone artifact — if part of GitHub's tolerance
for a given tag/attribute rests on THEIR CSP catching what the sanitizer
lets through, copying the list without the CSP copies the permissiveness
and leaves the backstop behind, WIDENING Farm Table's policy on a safety
argument that doesn't transfer. **The research phase must establish which
of GitHub's controls the policy depends on — #180/CSP may turn out to be a
PREREQUISITE for the sanitizer round, not a parallel track.** EM explicitly
did not assert this as fact, citing its own recent history of naming a
single cause when several existed (same discipline as the #194 "one gate"
mistakes) — but correctly insisted the round can't be scoped as if
separability is a given until checked.

I validated this at length: a security posture is not separable into
components you can copy piecemeal without checking what each was leaning
on, and the concrete evidence (no CSP + long-lived token) is exactly the
condition under which a widened allow-list would be riskiest.

### Constraint 2: the pin goes stale by construction — form 11 with roles swapped
"Matches GitHub's comment policy" is a claim about an EXTERNAL ARTIFACT that
changes on a schedule nobody here controls; GitHub hardens their sanitizer
over time, Farm Table's copy will not follow, and nothing in the tree would
notice divergence. **"That is a comment that goes false on a scheduled
event... form (11) with the roles swapped: not our oracle's target moving
after it looks, but our REFERENCE STANDARD moving while our copy of it
stands still."** Deliverable: pin a DATED, VERSIONED snapshot of what
GitHub's policy WAS when measured, with provenance for how it was
determined. State it as a snapshot; NEVER write a comment claiming ONGOING
equivalence, since that sentence is false the first time GitHub ships a
change and true-looking forever after (form 7's shape, arriving again).

Both constraints explicitly NOT pushback on ptone's product call — EM's own
framing, endorsed: it replaces an open design question with a researchable,
falsifiable one, strictly better than what task #18 had before. Neither
constraint affects anything currently running.

canonical preserve refs 0 -> 3; objects 5030 -> 10614. Every AFTER figure read
directly out of canonical, NOT from the fetch command's own success output.
Negative control (`0b52dcd`, unfetched lineage) still returns ABSENT, so the
method is falsifiable and the PASSes carry information.

### THE FINDING OF THE NIGHT: an expectation and an observation sharing a root
I attached two constraints to step 0. Constraint 2 (pre-register the expected
number, verify independently) is the one that paid.

EM had told me "641 insertions / 103 deletions across 7 files." I quoted it back
in my ruling AND relayed it to ptone. **The number was wrong**: 641/103 covers
only the SIX tracked-modified files; the new 581-line `remotedata_depth_test.go`
is IN ADDITION. Correct: 7 files / 1222 / 103. EM caught it while WRITING the
pre-registration and re-registered 1222 before running anything.

**Had it pre-registered 641 and observed 641, it would have preserved the
snapshot MINUS the single most valuable artefact in it and reported PASS.**

Named precisely, because it is NOT a false green — every number would have been
TRUE. The defect: expectation and observation were derived from the SAME upstream
mistake, so their agreement carried zero information. **A pre-registered number
only tests something if it is derived INDEPENDENTLY of the thing it checks;
otherwise it is a mirror, not a control.** Worse here because the wrong number
had been laundered through two apparently-independent sources (EM -> me -> ptone)
before being checked, so it would have looked corroborated.

Same root as EM's negative-control error ten minutes later: it predicted
`158c8ae` ABSENT, got `commit`, because 158c8ae is an ancestor of
`label-write-scope-r11` and fetching a branch fetches its ancestry. **An apparent
control that shares a dependency with its subject.** Filed as ONE finding with
two worked examples. EM's generalization, adopted: a negative control must come
from a DISJOINT LINEAGE — in a repo where every branch descends from one main,
"different agent" almost never means "different history."

### Technique worth keeping: snapshotting a live leg without disturbing it
Committing the dirty tree would change what `dev-xss-r4` finds on resume. EM
copied `.git/index` to /tmp, pointed `GIT_INDEX_FILE` at the copy, and ran
`git add -A` — objects land in the object DB, only the temp index moves. Working
tree, real index and HEAD provably byte-identical after (sha256 of `git status
--porcelain` before/after, HEAD still d12f572). `.gitignore` respected, so
web/dist and node_modules stayed out. Snapshot commit message states in plain
words that it is a preservation artefact, not authored by the leg and not on any
branch, so nobody later mistakes 27e0ee0 for the leg's own commit. Asked EM to
write this up in em-tooling as the standard way to snapshot a live leg.

### BINDING DISPATCH POLICY (until I lift it)
1. **ONE three-way round at a time.** r4 review first; **#194 r11 HELD**, no longer parallel.
2. **At most ONE agent executing a build or suite at any moment, PROJECT-WIDE** — not one
   per round, one total.
3. **One shared baseline run per round.** The test leg runs the suite and publishes the
   measurement **with the SHA it was taken at**; review and audit CONSUME it. That is the 3x
   reduction and it is where nearly all the load is.
4. **Targeted re-runs still allowed and are the point** — any leg may demand a specific
   re-run for a specific claim, but must ask, and re-runs are **serialized**.

   thoroughness win.**

### Why 3 does not cost review independence (the objection I pre-empted for the EM)
**THE THREE LEGS MUST BE INDEPENDENT IN ANALYSIS, AND A TEST RUN IS NOT AN ANALYSIS — IT IS
A MEASUREMENT.** What must stay independent is what each leg chooses to test and how it
interprets the result; sharing one measurement of the same SHA does not converge those. It
**would** cost independence if a leg were forbidden its own run — **which is why rule 4 is
not optional.**
**Caveat I imposed:** r4 measured a **4.50% flake rate** concentrated in `TestWatchTasks_*`.
**A single shared run bakes one sample of that flake into three legs at once — worse than
three independent single runs.** So the shared baseline is **RUN TWICE, both published.**
Still a third of the load of three concurrent runs.

1. **THE GUARDRAILS ARE PER-CONTAINER; THE FAILURE WAS AGGREGATE.** A per-container cap does
   not bound the sum unless the NUMBER of concurrent builders is bounded — eight containers

   each build, WIDENING the window in which builds overlap.** Necessary, not sufficient;
   admission control is what closes it. **Do not read the cap as permission to go wide.**

3. **The concurrency limit is currently enforced by me telling the EM to obey it — the

## 2026-07-29 00:12 — ptone corrected my guardrail pushback. He is right; conceded.

**ptone:** *"the per container limits will help because a single container could still grab
unlimited resources."*

**Correct, and a mode I skipped past. ONE uncapped container running `go build ./...` plus a
full suite can take the box on its own — the aggregate case is not required for the outage.
The cap closes a single-actor mode that NO amount of admission control would touch, because
admitting one is always allowed.** I argued it does not close the *aggregate* mode and let
that read as though it closed nothing.

**THE SPLIT, recorded: THE CAP BOUNDS WHAT ONE AGENT CAN DO; THE QUEUE BOUNDS HOW MANY CAN
DO IT. Different failure modes, neither substitutes for the other.**

### The consequence that matters operationally, and it is new
**The caps change what going wrong LOOKS like.** Before: overload ended in a **lockup** —
loud, unmistakable, took the control plane with it. With caps: the same overload appears as
**builds simply getting slow, and nothing crashes.** Much safer and **considerably harder to
notice**, because the natural reading of a slow build is "this suite is heavy," not "we are
oversubscribed."
**Standing: unexplained build slowness is a LOAD SIGNAL, not an annoyance.**

### Instrumentation ordered (EM, folded into the r4 grants — cheap, no new tooling)
- **Time every build granted; record wall-clock per run alongside the SHA in the queue log.**
- EM is the only party that sees runs **across** legs rather than within one, and **a per-leg
  observer cannot distinguish "my build is slow" from "the box is loaded" — the
  aggregate-versus-local class again, fourth instance, and the first one we can instrument
  BEFORE it costs anything rather than after.**
- Two signals: (1) a build materially slower than the same target's previous run;
  (2) **any two grants whose windows overlap when the queue says they should not** — that
  second one is the queue self-checking, and it is **the closest thing to a positive control
  the queue can have: a queue that has never observed an overlap has not been shown capable
  of detecting one.**
- **Caps stretch each build, so the overlap window is now WIDER than before. Serialization
  matters MORE under caps, not less.**

### THREE INSTRUMENT FAILURES, IN ORDER, EACH CAUGHT ONLY BY A CONTROL
1. **REFERENCES AND SCANNED VALUES WERE HASHED BY DIFFERENT FUNCTIONS.** `grep -o | sha256sum`
   hashes match+newline; `printf %s | sha256sum` does not. So the comparison **could not fire on
   any input**. It reported REAL_TOKEN_OCCURRENCES=0 over 16,423 files. A zero that was not a
   measurement of the corpus — it was a property of the arithmetic.
2. **FLATTENING DESTROYS TOKEN BOUNDARIES.** `tr -d '\n'` joins the token to its neighbours; the
   greedy class `[A-Za-z0-9_]*` then swallows the following word into the match. Wrap-proofing
   (required by #91) and identity-by-value are in DIRECT CONFLICT. Remedy: do not extract
   greedily — anchor at the prefix and take EXACTLY the known width.
3. **A `for` loop over an unmatched zsh glob aborts the whole command**, leaving `scanned=0,
   hits=0` — which reads as a clean sweep. Visible only because I had not muted stderr.

a token with no alphanumeric neighbour is the arrangement in which greedy extraction is harmless.

## #153 — THE CLASS THAT REFRAMES THE WHOLE FUNNEL (provision-writable's, generalised)

`--all --not --glob=refs/remotes/*` excludes everything reachable from a remote-tracking ref, and
those refs point at a directory on this disk. **What the filter certifies about an excluded commit
is "reachable from a ref in a local store" — ON-HOST REPLICATION, NOT OFF-HOST DURABILITY.** Applied
to the funnel end to end: 348 → 222 dropped as contained in a local bundle *file* → 126 → 0
contained in any "remote" that resolved to a local path. **If the bundles live on this host, every
filter in the chain measures on-host redundancy and the funnel is silent on the question it was
built to answer.** A bundle on the same disk as the repository it protects is a copy, not a backup —
and this project exists because a host locked up.

**THE ONLY OFF-HOST FACT ESTABLISHED TONIGHT:** 268 objects fetched back from scion-repo-contrib
into a virgin bare repo with `objects/info/alternates` confirmed absent.

Packet consequence, stated plainly: *"126 at risk if this host dies"* and *"126 not present in any
local bundle"* are different sentences, **and I have been writing the first while holding evidence
for the second.**

## THE .gitignore HOLE (#155) — A DURABILITY HOLE UNDER THE FREEZE'S OWN PREMISE

`.gitignore:17` is `dist/` with no leading slash → matches **at any depth**. One rule; no other
ignore file in the repo; no `web/.gitignore`. Confirmed twice with discriminating controls (EM:
`web/dist/x` matched, `src/util/dist/deep.ts` matched, `src/build/telemetry.ts` not; ci-22: six
depths matched, with `Makefile`, `web/src/main.ts`, `internal/server/watch_test.go` and the
near-miss decoys `distant/x`, `notdist/x` all correctly not matched).

**WHEN IT FIRES IT FIRES SILENTLY:** `git add -A` succeeds, status is clean, review sees nothing,
the file is not in the commit, and there is no record it ever existed. **Worse than a stranded
commit, which can at least be fetched.** Current population ENUMERATED 0 = 0 + 0 — **the zero is the
finding, not the reassurance.**

**RULED: NO .gitignore CHANGE TONIGHT.** Anchoring to `/dist/` un-ignores `web/dist`, whose
`go:embed` dependency is unmeasured (#13); main is red; two gate steps have never executed on main;
it is eight in the morning. An obvious one-line fix landed now is how the next defect gets in.
Detection ordered instead, read-only: `git status --ignored` per tree, filtered to dist-component
paths that are not `web/dist`, three integers plus a path list.

**THE VERIFICATION TRAP THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE FINDING:** `git check-ignore -v web/dist` reports
**NOT IGNORED**. A trailing-slash pattern matches directories only, and check-ignore decides
directory-ness **by looking at disk**; in a fresh clone the path does not exist, so it is treated as
a file and the rule does not match — rc=0, no warning, opposite conclusion. Ask about a path
**inside** the directory. **The instrument gives the reassuring answer precisely in the clean clone
where nobody has built yet.** A finding whose obvious verification refutes it will be refuted by the
first careful person who checks.

## ADDENDUM 08:01Z–08:13Z — THE 126 IS CONFIRMED AT 126 AGAINST THE LIVE SERVER

**limitation 6 is CLOSED BY MEASUREMENT, and the census's 0 was right for better reasons than its
method could guarantee.** Two independent live mechanisms, relocate-offhost, report §19:

1. **Set intersection** against `/tmp/inv/srv2.git` — fetched **by URL**, 216 refs **including
   `refs/pull/*`** (which is what retains force-pushed-away work), 600-commit closure → **0 hits.**
2. **Fetch-by-SHA, capability established BEFORE any negative was read**: control tip `cc927355`
   rc=0; **control NON-TIP `7a0f220` rc=0** → `allowReachableSHA1InWant` is ENABLED. Five of the 126
   sampled → all rc=128 *"not our ref"*.

Controls both ways: `cc927355` tip True, `7a0f220` True, three further ancestors of main True,
all-zeros SHA False. **The non-tip positives are the load-bearing ones** — a commit stranded by a
force-push is by construction not any ref's tip, so a tip-only control proves the method works on
the one case it will never meet.

**BOUND STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER:** `allowReachableSHA1InWant` only serves *reachable*
non-tip SHAs, which the set intersection already covers. Detecting **present-but-unreachable** on
the server needs `allowAnySHA1InWant`, a separate switch, **and no known unreachable-but-present
server SHA exists to build a positive control from.** So *"not our ref"* cannot distinguish *the
server does not have it* from *the server will not serve unreachable SHAs*. **It told me the
negative cannot discriminate rather than substituting a method that returns something.** Its
judgement, labelled as judgement and accepted: an object present-but-unreachable on GitHub is
subject to GitHub's own gc — the same condition these commits are already in, on someone else's
disk. Not durability.

objects nobody else has. The classes most likely to be dropped from an enumeration are the classes
most likely to matter.**

## V1 vs V2 — MATCH V2, AND RECORD THE REASON RATHER THAN THE CHOICE

V2 (`--no-reflogs`) counts reflog-reachable objects as unreachable — the **conservative** direction,
and the right one here specifically because **this host's reflogs survive only by a config setting
imposed tonight** (`gc.reflogExpire=never`, `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable=never`).

  **A MEASUREMENT THAT IS ONLY TRUE WHILE AN EMERGENCY CONTROL IS IN FORCE MUST SAY SO NEXT TO THE
  NUMBER.**
